title: 简简单单写程序
summary: The goal and workflow of programming, your first programs, simple arithmetic, variables and constants.

boxes.text: A program is a list of exact steps that turns the **input** into the required **output**.
Most of your time goes into the last two steps: testing on the samples, then on small cases you make up yourself.
A missing `;`, a wrong bracket or a misspelt name is a **compile error**: the program does not run at all. Read the first error message. Its line number points at the mistake, or just after it.
A raw string `R"(...)"` prints everything between the brackets exactly as typed. It is the easy way through picture problems like P1000, B2025 and B2005.
`#define int long long`: printf needs `%lld`, and the largest value is `LLONG_MAX`, not `INT_MAX`.
`#define double long double`: `printf("%f", x)` silently prints 0.000000. Use `cout << fixed << setprecision(k)` instead.
`#define endl '\n'`: endl no longer flushes. In an interactive problem, call `cout.flush()` after every question you send.
C++ works out arithmetic like a calculator: brackets first, then `* / %`, then `+ -`. Within one level it goes left to right.
Word problems like P2433 小学数学 N 合一 are all this: turn each sentence into one expression, and choose integer or real division on purpose.
`pow` returns a double, so a big integer power can be off by one. Multiply in a loop instead. `sqrt` returns a double too.
A **variable** is a named box that holds one value of a fixed type.
`swap(a, b)` does the same three moves for you.
`=` stores a value, `==` compares two. A variable you never gave a value holds garbage, so always set it before use.

title: 顺序结构程序设计
summary: Data types, input and output, worked sequential programs, and how to read a judge verdict and check your own code.

boxes.text: Every variable has a **type**. The type decides how many bytes it gets, and so which values fit.
Overflow does not crash. An int that passes 2.1 × 10⁹ **silently** becomes a wrong number. When in doubt, use long long and write constants as `100000LL`.
`double(a / b)` is still 3.0: the integer division already happened. And `long long x = a * b;` still overflows when a and b are int, because the product is made as an int first.
scanf needs `&`: `scanf("%d", &n)`. Reading a long long with `%d`, or a double with `%f` (use `%lf`), gives garbage.
Time problems: convert to minutes, compute, then convert back with `/ 60` and `% 60`. Going back past midnight needs `(t % 1440 + 1440) % 1440`. This is P1425 and P5707.
The judge runs your program on hidden tests. Each verdict points to a different kind of mistake, so read it before you change any code.
Debug values go to `cerr`, so the judge never sees them. Still remove them before you submit: printing takes time.
Samples pass but a hidden test is WA? It is usually an edge case or overflow. Make a tiny test you can solve by hand, and compare.

title: 分支结构程序设计
summary: Relational and logical expressions, if/else and switch, nested branches, and worked branching programs.

boxes.text: A comparison such as `x > 3` is a value of type **bool**: true (printed as 1) or false (0).
**Short circuit**: && stops at the first false part, || at the first true part. So `n != 0 && a / n > 2` never divides by zero.
`if (a = b)` assigns instead of comparing. And `1 < x < 5` means `(1 < x) < 5`, which is always true.
`if (x);` has an empty body: the `;` ends the if. An else pairs with the nearest if, so use braces.
An else if chain tests its conditions **in order** and runs only the first one that is true.
Leap year: divisible by 4 and not by 100, or divisible by 400. In one line: `(y % 4 == 0 && y % 100 != 0) || y % 400 == 0`.
Each case needs `break`, or it falls through into the next. `x = cond ? a : b` picks one of two values.
An if inside another if makes a **decision tree**: the inner question is only asked on one branch of the outer one.
Many nests flatten into one else if chain with &&. That is often easier to read.
Without braces, `if (a) if (b) x; else y;` attaches the else to the **inner** if, whatever the indentation says. Brace every nested if.
Every test stays in integers, so there is no rounding error. Sorting first removes the "which side is longest" cases.
Work out the cost of every choice and keep the smallest. Start the minimum at `LLONG_MAX`, or at the first choice. This is P1909.
`0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is false for doubles. Compare with a tolerance, `fabs(x - y) < 1e-9`, or multiply out so everything stays an integer.

title: 循环结构程序设计
summary: for and while loops, nested loops, and loop patterns: running values, digits, primes, simulation and brute force.

boxes.text: A **loop** repeats its body. Before every round it checks a condition, and it stops as soon as that condition is false.
`break` leaves the innermost loop at once. `continue` skips to the next round: in a for the update still runs, in a while it does not, which can loop forever.
Many problems need only a few **running values**, updated once per input. No array is needed when each number is used once.
Building `rev * 10 + digit` reverses the number, and trailing zeros vanish on their own (P1307). Use do while so that 0 still counts as one digit.
When the number of rounds is unknown, loop with while on the stopping condition and count the rounds. This solves P1423, P1035 and P1089.
The outer loop picks a row, the inner loop fills it. Write the inner bound in terms of the outer variable to get a **triangle**.
Reset a per row counter **inside** the outer loop, not before it.
`break` leaves only the innermost loop. To stop both, set a flag and test it in the outer condition, as above. Tighten bounds such as `a * a <= n` when you can.
If n = a × b with a ≤ b, then a ≤ √n. So testing divisors while `i * i <= n` is enough: O(√n) instead of O(n).
Euclid: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`, ending when b is 0. C++17 has `gcd(a, b)` built in.
Put the **cheap** test (is it a palindrome? about 8 steps) before the **expensive** one (is it prime? up to √x steps). Most numbers fail the cheap test, so the slow one rarely runs.
Every palindrome with an even number of digits divides by 11, so 11 is the only prime among them. Skipping those ranges makes b up to 10⁸ fast enough (P1217).
Rule of thumb: about **10⁸** simple operations per second. Estimate the loop count from the limits before you write code.

title: 数组与数据批量存储
summary: One-dimensional and multi-dimensional arrays, and the standard array techniques used in contest problems.

boxes.text: One variable holds only its last value. An **array** keeps every value, and because the index is a variable, a loop can reach any box in any order.
`int a[N]` has boxes `a[0]` to `a[N-1]`. There is no `a[N]`.
A local array is not zeroed: write `= {}` or call `fill`. With many test cases, reset only the first n boxes with `fill(a, a + n, 0)`, not the whole array each time.
Declare big arrays **global**: they start at 0 and do not overflow the stack. Size with a margin: `int a[1005]` for n ≤ 1000.

Reading past the end (`a[n]`, `a[-1]`) does not crash reliably. It reads a neighbour or garbage, and the bug shows up far away. A reverse loop that starts at `i = n` prints one value that was never filled.
Think of a **table**: the first index picks the row, the second the column. Read and print with two nested loops, rows outside and columns inside.
`int g[105][105]` is about 44 KB. A grid of characters is easiest as `string g[N]`: read one row with `cin >> g[i]`, and `g[i][j]` is still row i, column j.
The outer loop is the screen row, the inner loop walks the items. This is P5730.
Record: `mark[p] = 1` says position p has some property. Setting it twice leaves it at 1, so overlaps are handled for free.
Counter: `cnt[v]++` says you saw value v once more. One step per value, no searching.
Counting by value also sorts: walk the indexes in order and print each value cnt times.
Every element against every other: outer `i`, inner `j = i + 1`. That visits each pair **exactly once**, and never an element with itself.
n(n − 1) / 2 pairs is O(n²): fine up to n ≈ 5000.
A value made by several pairs is still counted once, which is what "how many numbers" questions want (P2141).
Recomputing every window costs O(n·m). **Sliding** costs O(n): the next window is this one, plus the new right value, minus the old left one.
The zero padding in row 0 and column 0 makes every row start and end with 1, with no if (P5732).
A direction becomes a number d. Moving is `x += dx[d], y += dy[d]`. Turning right is `d = (d + 1) % 4`.
Check the bounds **before** reading `g[ni][nj]`. Or use 1 based storage with a padding border so every neighbour exists (P1789).
Write each transform as "where does cell (i, j) go?". Then 180° is 90° twice, and combinations are transforms applied one after another.
Never rotate **in place**: writing into `a` while still reading it destroys cells you need. Build the result in a second array, then copy it back (P1205).
Store a 0 and 1 sequence as the **lengths of its runs**. By convention the first run counts 0s, so a sequence starting with 1 begins with a run of length 0 (P1319, P1320).

title: 字符串与文件操作
summary: Character arrays, the string type and its toolkit, and reading and writing files and redirection.

boxes.text: A **character array** stores text one character per box, followed by an invisible end marker `'\0'`. You walk it until you meet that marker.
Read a whole line into a char array with `cin.getline(a, 105)`. Size the array one larger than the longest text, for the end marker.
Writing past the end, or forgetting the `'\0'` when you build text yourself, makes `cout << a` print garbage after the text.
Letters and digits have consecutive codes, so each test is one range comparison. Writing to `s[i]` changes the string itself.
Map the letter to 0…25, do the arithmetic, wrap with `% 26`, map back. Shifting backwards can go negative, so add 26 before the last `% 26` (P1914).
`cnt[ch - 'a']++` is a counting array with the **letter as the index**. Ignore letters that never appear when you look for the minimum (P1125).
A letter's value 1 to 26 is `ch - 'A' + 1`. A product of such values mod 47 is kept small with `p = p * v % 47` at every step (P1200).
`strlen(a)` in a loop condition recounts the string every round: O(n²). Store it once.
Mixing scanf or printf with cin or cout is only safe without the fast IO line (`fast` in your template).
`s.size()` is **unsigned**: on an empty string, `s.size() - 1` is 18446744073709551615, not −1. Write `int(s.size()) - 1`, or check `s.empty()` first.
After `cin >> x`, the rest of that line is still waiting. The next getline returns it. Fix: one extra getline to throw it away.
Files made on Windows end lines with `\r\n`, and getline keeps the `\r`. Skip it when you count or compare characters (P5015).
`find` returns an unsigned size_t. Compare it with `string::npos`, not with -1.
`<` on strings compares letter by letter, like a dictionary: `"10" < "9"` is true. Convert to numbers first.
To match **whole words** only, lowercase both strings and put a space on both ends of each. Then `" be "` cannot match inside bee or maybe.
`p = find(w, p + 1)` visits every match, overlapping ones too. Use `p + w.size()` when matches must not overlap (P1308).
Working on the digits as a string avoids overflow and keeps leading zeros under your control (P1553).
Build each row as a string and trim trailing spaces before printing (P1598).
To glue strings into the smallest result, put x first when `x + y < y + x`. The `[](…) {…}` is a small inline comparison function, a lambda (P1603).
Normally a program reads the keyboard and prints to the screen. Files can take their place: either the program opens them itself, or the command line **redirects** the keyboard and screen.
An ifstream is used exactly like cin, and an ofstream exactly like cout. Only the name changes.
Redirection needs no code changes, so it is the quickest way to rerun a long sample. Compare outputs with fc or diff, not by eye.
Comment out freopen when testing by hand, or the program waits on a file. Luogu reads standard input: submit without freopen unless the problem asks for files.

title: 函数与结构体
summary: Defining functions, scope and parameter passing, recursion, and structs with sorting.

boxes.text: A **function** packs a computation under a name. You write the logic once, test it once, and call it as often as you like.
Write the side length once as a function instead of copying the formula three times (P5735). One fix in the function fixes every call.
Calling a function defined **below** main, with no declaration above, gives "was not declared in this scope". Put helpers above main, or declare them first.
A non void function must return on every path. Falling off the end returns garbage, and the compiler only warns.
A **lambda**, `[](int x) { return x * x * x; }`, is a small unnamed function written where it is used. You met one as the comparison in sort.
A bool helper can return as soon as the answer is known: `return false` inside the loop stops the whole function.
Once isPrime exists, "write each even number as a sum of two primes, smallest first" is two loops and one test (P1304).
Reuse helpers across problems: the same isPrime solves P5736, P1304, P1217 and P1075. Keep a tested copy in your notes.
By default a parameter is a **copy**: changing it inside does not touch the caller. Add `&` to make it a **reference**, another name for the caller's variable.
Use `&` to change arguments (swap) or to send back several results. Use `const string &s` to pass a big object without copying it and without changing it.
An array argument is **never copied**: the function works on the caller's array. Pass the length n along with it, and write const when it should only read.
A local with the same name as a global **hides** it. Give globals clear names. `::cnt` reaches the global when you must.
A recursive function has a **base case** that answers directly, and a **recursive case** that calls itself on a smaller input. Each call waits on a stack until the call it made returns.
No base case, or a step that does not shrink the input, means infinite recursion: a stack overflow crash. Very deep recursion, around 10⁵ to 10⁶ levels, can crash too.
Recursion fits when the answer for n is built from the answer for a smaller n (P5739, P5743). Any such recursion can also be a loop: recursion is shorter, the loop avoids deep stacks.
Split the square into four quarters. One is handled directly; the other three are **the same problem at half size**. The function describes one level, and recursion repeats it (P5461).
Plain `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` recomputes the same values again and again: hopeless for n = 50.
Store each result the first time and return it straight away next time. Each fib(k) is then computed once: O(n). This "remember results" idea is the seed of dynamic programming.
Some answers need no recursion at all: the sum over all subsets is (sum of elements) × 2ⁿ⁻¹, because each element is in half of the subsets (P2415).
A **struct** is a new type made of named fields. One Student carries a name and three scores together, so sorting moves the whole record at once.
Fields use a dot: `s.name`. An array of structs, `Student a[1005]`, is a table with one row per student.
Using `>`, not `>=`, when searching for the best keeps the **first** student among ties (P5740). `Student &s = a[best]` gives a short name without copying.
Pass a struct by reference, `Person &p`, when the function should update it, and by `const Person &p` when it only reads. Passing by value copies every field.
`score * 1.2` uses floating point and can land just below the true value. `score * 6 / 5` stays exact in integers (P5744, P5742).
`sort(a, a + n, cmp)` calls `cmp(x, y)` to ask "must x come before y?". Compare the main key first; only on a tie, compare the next key.
cmp must be a **strict** order: return false when x and y are equal. Writing `>=` instead of `>` can crash sort.
Or give the struct an `operator<` and call plain `sort(a, a + n)`. For a one off order, a lambda works too.

title: 模拟与高精度
summary: Turning rules into code without slips, and arithmetic on numbers of any length.

boxes.text: A simulation has no clever trick. The difficulty is reading **every rule** correctly and turning it into code without slips.
Before coding: list every rule from the statement, note the edge cases (empty input, ties, wrap around), and check the output format character by character.
State: the two scores of the current game. Step: one character. Stop: one side reaches the target **and** leads by 2; the input ends at 'E'.
Store the input once, then run the same function for both rule sets, 11 and 21. Print the last, unfinished game even when it is 0:0 (P1042).
`cin >> ch` skips spaces and line breaks, which is exactly right here: the record can be split over many lines.
Number the seats 0 … n − 1. Moving s seats round the circle is `(p + s) % n` one way and `(p - s + n) % n` the other.
Facing in or out flips left and right. Instead of four cases, "facing direction equals instruction" always means the same way round: one comparison decides it (P1563).
`p - s` can be negative and % keeps the sign: add n first. If s can exceed n, reduce it with `s % n`.
Copy a rule table from the statement into a 2D array once. Then every round is a **lookup**, not a chain of ifs (P1328).
A pattern of length k that repeats forever: round i uses element `i % k`.

Grid simulations (P2670, P4924, P1518) reuse chapter 5's tools: dx and dy arrays, bounds checks, rotating into a second array. If a walk might never end, stop after a safe maximum or detect a repeated state.
Split the output into small decisions, one per rule: sign, coefficient, variable, power. Each decision is one if that matches one sentence of the statement (P1067).
String expansion (P1098) and work scheduling (P1065) are the same style: many small rules, each a separate, testable piece.
long long stops at about 9.2 × 10¹⁸. Longer numbers are kept as a vector of digits, **ones digit first**.

Every operation is the school method: work from the ones digit up, keep a carry or borrow, and remove leading zeros at the end. Read as a string, convert with toBig, compute, trim, print from the last index down.
Loop while either number has digits left **or** there is a carry. Each step: digit sum + carry; keep `% 10`, pass `/ 10` on (P1601).
Numbers of different lengths need no padding: a missing digit counts as 0.
Compare first: more digits means bigger; equal length, compare from the top digit down. Subtract the smaller from the larger, and add a minus sign if you swapped.
Borrow: when a digit goes negative, add 10 and take 1 from the next digit. trim afterwards, so 1000 − 999 prints 1, not 0001.
Multiplying by an ordinary int k touches each digit once: `digit × k + carry`. The final carry can be several digits long, so push them one by one.
`digit * k + carry` must fit in an int: fine for k up to about 10⁸. For bigger k use long long, or big × big.
Build each value from the previous one, k! = (k − 1)! × k, instead of recomputing from scratch. The same habit makes 2ᵖ cheap (P1045).
Digit i of a times digit j of b lands in **column i + j**. Add all products first, in long long, then sweep the carries once.
A product has at most len(a) + len(b) digits; trim removes the rest, so 0 × 12345 prints 0 (P1303). Cost: O(len(a) × len(b)).
Long division goes the other way, **from the top digit down**: bring down one digit into the remainder, write the quotient digit, keep the remainder.
Only the remainder is needed for "is this huge number divisible by k?". The digit count of 2ᵖ is ⌊p · log₁₀ 2⌋ + 1 (P1045).
A fixed array must be big enough for the longest answer: len(a) + len(b) + 1 digits for a product. A vector grows by itself.

title: 排序
summary: Counting sort, selection/bubble/insertion sort, quicksort, and applying sorting to problems.

boxes.text: When the values come from a **small range** (say 1 … 1000) but there are millions of them, tally them in a counting array and print each value as many times as it was seen. O(n + range), no comparisons at all (P1271).
Millions of numbers make input the bottleneck. Turn on fast IO (`fast` in your template), and never use endl per number.
For each position from the left, find the **smallest** value in the rest and swap it into place. At most n − 1 swaps, but always about n²/2 comparisons.
Walk the array, swapping **neighbours** that are out of order. After pass k the k largest values are in place at the end. Each swap fixes exactly one **inversion**: a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j].
Bubble sort swaps = inversions = the fewest neighbour swaps needed to sort (P1116). O(n²): fine for n up to a few thousand.
Keep a sorted prefix and slide each new value into place. **Fast when the data is almost sorted.**
All three are O(n²). Use them to understand or to count; use sort to sort.
Quicksort: pick a **pivot**, move smaller values left and bigger values right (partition), then sort the two sides the same way. About log n levels of O(n) work each.
The first element as pivot makes already sorted data O(n²). The middle element, or a random one, avoids that. P1177 includes such data on purpose; in practice just call sort.
To find only the k-th smallest, you need **just one side** after each partition: O(n) on average. The library does this as `nth_element`.
With 5 × 10⁶ numbers, slow input alone can time out: the two fast IO lines are required here (P1923).

Merge sort sorts each half, then merges two sorted lists by taking the smaller front value: always O(n log n). Taking from the right half jumps over everything left in the left half, which **counts inversions** in O(n log n).
`sort(a, a + n)` puts a[0] … a[n−1] in increasing order in O(n log n). After sorting, equal values sit next to each other, and the k-th smallest is at index k − 1.
The range is half open: first included, end excluded. For a 1 based array use `sort(a + 1, a + n + 1)`.
`unique` removes **adjacent** repeats, moving the kept values to the front, and erase cuts off the rest. It only works after sort makes all copies adjacent (P1059).
Small value range? A marking array does the same: `seen[x] = true`, then print every marked value in order.
Write the comparator as a **ladder**: compare key 1; if different, return that. Otherwise move to key 2, and so on. The last rung is usually the input order, an id you stored (P1093, P1068, P1786).
Need equal keys to keep input order? Add the id as the last key, or call `stable_sort` (P1104).
A comparator must be a strict order: `cmp(x, x)` must be false. Using `>=` or `<=` breaks sort, sometimes with a crash.
Cut off lines: sort, take the score at position ⌊m × 1.5⌋, then count everyone with a score ≥ that line, because ties at the line all pass (P1068).
Numbers too long for long long can still be compared: **more digits means bigger**; the same length means dictionary order (P1781).
`return x - y;` can overflow for large values of opposite sign. `(x > y) - (x < y)` is safe.

title: 暴力枚举
summary: Try every candidate, but count them first: loop enumeration, subset enumeration and permutation enumeration.

boxes.text: **Enumeration** tries every candidate and keeps the ones that pass a test. It is always correct if the list is complete, so the only question is speed. Count the candidates before you code.
Three ways to make enumeration fast enough: enumerate **fewer variables** and compute the last one; **tighten the bounds** of each loop; **change what you enumerate**.
Enumerating sizes is O(nm): 25 million steps for 5000 × 5000 (P2241).
Choosing all nine digits is 9! = 362 880 arrangements. Once the first number x is known, the ratio fixes the other two, so only about 900 values of x need testing (P1618).
A `bool seen[10]` array checks "each digit once" in one pass.
For A + B = C only A and B are free: C = A + B. With at most 24 sticks every number stays below about 1111, so two loops of about 1100 suffice (P1149).
Get the bound from the limits, then test it: a bigger bound must not change any answer. More practice: P3392, P3654, P3799.
A set of n items has 2ⁿ subsets. Number them 0 … 2ⁿ − 1 and read each in binary: **bit i is 1 when item i is chosen**. One loop visits every subset once.
Test bit i with `mask >> i & 1`. `1 << n` is 2ⁿ. n ≤ 20 gives about a million subsets.
Each level decides one item: **take** it, recurse, then **undo** and try the next. Taking only later numbers lists every combination once, in dictionary order (P1157).
Take, recurse, undo is the heart of backtracking (chapter 14).
A permutation is an ordering of all n items; there are n! (10! = 3 628 800). `next_permutation` steps to the next ordering in dictionary order.
It returns false after the largest ordering. Starting unsorted skips every smaller ordering: **sort first**, and use do … while so the first one prints too (P1706).
Fill the positions one at a time; `used[v]` remembers which values are taken. The recursive form can **prune**: stop a branch as soon as it breaks a rule.
Ten ingredients of 1, 2 or 3 grams adding up to n: at most 3¹⁰ = 59 049 recipes. If even all 1s left would exceed n, or all 3s could not reach it, stop that branch (P2089).

First Step ( ファーストステップ )

title: 递推与递归
summary: Build answers bottom-up from smaller ones (recurrence), or top-down by solving the same problem on smaller input (recursion).

boxes.text: **Recurrence** (递推) builds the answer for size i from answers already found for smaller sizes, filling a table from the bottom up. Write down all four parts before coding.

The values grow like Fibonacci numbers: f[5000] has over 1000 digits, so the table holds big numbers from chapter 8 (P1255). Only the last two entries are needed, so two variables replace the whole table.
A pawn moves only right or down. Ways to reach a cell = ways to the cell **above** + ways to the cell on the **left**. Blocked cells (✕) have 0 ways. Fill row by row, so both neighbours are ready.
In the starting grid, 9 = 5 (above) + 4 (left). The first row and first column have exactly 1 way each until a blocked cell cuts them off.
Shifting every coordinate by 1 gives the table a row 0 and column 0 of zeros, so the edges need no special case. The counts reach about 10¹⁷ on a 20 × 20 board: use `long long` (P1002).
Stack output orders split by where the first element leaves: f[i] = Σ f[k] · f[i−1−k], the Catalan numbers (P1044). "Prepend a number at most half of the current one" sums f[1 … i/2] (P1028).
Count the ways to spend exactly m on distinct dishes. Add dishes one at a time; with dish a, every amount j gains the ways that reached j − a before (P1164).
Loop j **downwards**. Going upwards would let the same dish be used again within one round.
Tiling a 2 × n wall with dominoes and L shapes: list how the right end can look, and write one transition per shape (P1990).

**Recursion** (递归) writes the answer in terms of the same problem on smaller input, top down. It suits nested structure: brackets inside brackets, a board split into quarters, a string built from copies of itself.
To move n disks, trust the function to move n − 1: clear them to the spare peg, move the largest, then bring the n − 1 back. The base case n = 0 does nothing. The count is 2ⁿ − 1.

Write the recursive call as if it already works for smaller n; then only one level has to be right. Moving black and white pieces into alternate order (P1259) has the same "solve n from n − 1" structure.
The plain recursion calls itself several times per level and explodes. Only 20 × 20 × 20 different arguments can occur, so store each result the first time (P1464).
Keep the guard order exactly as the statement gives it: the "≤ 0" rule comes before the "> 20" rule.

A bracket inside the text is the same problem again: the decoder calls itself at "[" and returns at the matching "]" (P1928). An exponent written in powers of 2 is again "write a number in powers of 2" (P1010).

Each doubling appends a copy rotated by one place. A position in the second half maps back to one position in the first half, so halve until it lies inside the original string: O(log n) steps even for n = 10¹⁸ (P3612).

Board and picture problems split the same way: a 2ᵏ board with one missing cell is covered by one L shape in the centre plus four quarters (P1228); the totem picture is three copies of the smaller picture (P1498).

title: 贪心
summary: Take the best-looking choice at each step, and prove it is safe: exchange arguments, interval scheduling, and Huffman coding.

boxes.text: A greedy algorithm builds the answer one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never undoing it. It is short and fast, but only correct when you can prove that a locally best choice never spoils the overall best answer.

Two standard proofs. Exchange argument: take any optimal answer that differs from the greedy one, swap one piece to match greedy, and show it gets no worse. Stays ahead: after every step, greedy is at least as good as any other method so far.
With coins 4, 3, 1, greedy pays 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 needs only two. "Take the biggest coin" is correct for some coin systems (1, 2, 5, 10 …) and wrong for others.
Before trusting a greedy rule, compare it with a slow brute force on many small random inputs (a stress test). One mismatch kills the rule; no mismatches is evidence, and then look for the proof.
Gold dust can be split, so value per unit weight is all that matters: take the richest pile first, then the next, and cut the last one to fit (P2240).
Compare ratios v₁/w₁ > v₂/w₂ as v1 * w2 > v2 * w1 : exact in integers. When items cannot be split (0/1 knapsack), this greedy is wrong; that needs dynamic programming.

Swapping two neighbours changes only their own waits, so any order with a longer job before a shorter one can be improved by a swap. Hence sorted by time is optimal (P1223). pair sorts by the first field, then the second; t[i].first and t[i].second read the two fields.

Taking the contest that ends first leaves the most time for the rest; any optimal plan can swap its first contest for this one without losing anything (P1803). Sorting by start time or by length both fail on small examples.

Smallest number after deleting k digits: whenever a digit is larger than the one after it, deleting it helps most, because it sits in a higher place (P1106). Filling pits: a day of work covers one continuous stretch, so only each rise from the previous depth costs extra days (P5019).

Pairing: the most expensive souvenir must leave; let it take the cheapest one with it if they fit; two pointers after sorting (P1094). Adjacent sums: when a pair is too large, eating from the right box also lowers the next pair, so it is never worse (P3817).

Biggest number from concatenation: sort with a + b > b + a (P1012). The king's game sorts ministers by a × b and needs big numbers (P1080). Picking cheapest first (P1208, P1478) and alternating tallest and shortest jumps (P4995) are sort-then-scan greedies; prove each with an exchange of two neighbours.

Huffman coding gives frequent characters short codes and rare ones long codes. Build a tree: repeatedly take the two smallest weights, join them under a new node whose weight is their sum, and put it back. Each character's code length is its depth.
The total cost (sum of frequency × code length) equals the sum of all the joined weights. Why greedy works: the two rarest symbols can always be placed deepest, as siblings, in some optimal tree.

priority_queue keeps the largest element on top; with greater<long long> it keeps the smallest. push and pop cost O(log n), so n merges cost O(n log n) (P1090: merging fruit heaps is exactly a Huffman tree).
Sorting once is not enough: each merged heap must go back among the others, possibly in the middle. That is why a priority queue is used.

Store the tree as a parent array: leaves are 0 … n − 1, each merge creates the next node number. Following parents up from a leaf gives its depth, which is its code length. Check: 5·4 + 9·4 + 12·3 + 13·3 + 16·3 + 45·1 = 224.

title: 二分查找与二分答案
summary: Halve the range: find a boundary in a sorted array, a root of a function, or the best answer whose check is monotone.

boxes.text: In a sorted array the test "a[i] ≥ x" is false for a prefix and true for the rest. Binary search finds the boundary by halving the range: look at the middle, keep the half that still contains the boundary. log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20 steps instead of 10⁶.
Use one template and its invariant always: lo is always bad (or −1), hi is always good (or n). The loop ends when they are neighbours, and hi is the first good index.
Templates mixing lo <= hi , mid + 1 and mid - 1 loop forever or miss by one when you change one detail. The hi - lo > 1 form never does: mid is always strictly between lo and hi.

lower_bound(b, e, x) points to the first element ≥ x, upper_bound to the first element > x; both need sorted data and run in O(log n). Their difference counts the copies of x (P1102). The closest value to g is the element at lower_bound or the one just before it (P1678).
A continuous function that changes sign on [lo, hi] has a root there. Halving keeps the half where the sign still changes. Roots at least 1 apart means each unit interval holds at most one (P1024).
For real numbers, loop a fixed number of times (60 halvings shrink any range far below 10−9) instead of comparing with an epsilon. Interest rates (P1163) and times (P3743) are searched the same way.
Binary search on the answer: when the question is "the largest (or smallest) x that works", and works(x) is monotone (if x works, every smaller x works too), search over x instead of over an array.
Recipe: (1) say what x is; (2) prove monotonicity in one sentence; (3) write check(x) , usually a greedy O(n) scan; (4) pick lo (surely works) and hi (surely fails) and run the template.

A higher saw gives less wood, so "enough wood" holds up to some height and fails above it (P1873). Longer pieces give fewer pieces (P2440). Both checks are one O(n) loop; with about 30 halvings the whole solution is O(n log range).

"Make the smallest jump as large as possible" and "make the largest part as small as possible" are the classic signals for binary search on the answer. The check is a greedy pass: keep a stone only if it is far enough (P2678); start a new part only when the sum would exceed the cap (P1182). Road signs that shrink the longest gap (P3853) follow the same pattern.

Note which side is good in each problem: maximising keeps lo good and outputs lo ; minimising keeps hi good and outputs hi . Pick the starting lo and hi so the invariant is already true before the loop.

title: 搜索
summary: Depth-first search with backtracking for every solution, and breadth-first search for the fewest steps.

boxes.text: Depth-first search (DFS) explores one choice all the way down before trying the next. When a branch fails or is finished, it backtracks: undoes the last choice and tries another. Written as recursion, the call stack remembers where to come back to.
Template: check the goal; for each possible move: if allowed, mark it, recurse, unmark it. Forgetting to unmark is the most common backtracking bug.

One queen per row, so the recursion goes row by row. Each column and each diagonal holds at most one queen: cells on the same "/" diagonal have the same r + c, cells on the same "\" diagonal have the same r − c (shifted by n so the index is not negative). Three boolean arrays make every check O(1) (P1219).
To count all paths that never revisit a cell, mark a cell when you step on it and unmark it when you step back, so later paths may use it again (P1605).
This explores every path, which grows exponentially: fine for a 5 × 5 maze, hopeless for 50 × 50. For the shortest path use BFS (14.2) instead.

Keeping each part at least as large as the one before (minPart ) lists every split exactly once and already in order (P2404). The same "choose → recurse → undo" lists subsets (选数 P1036, PERKET P2036, 第10章).

Pruning cuts branches that cannot win: stop when the partial cost already exceeds the best answer found (吃奶酪 P1433), or when the remaining choices cannot reach the goal. Order choices so good answers are found early, which makes the cut stronger.

Scan the grid; each time you meet unvisited water, that is a new lake, and a DFS "sinks" every connected cell so it is not counted again (P1596). No unmarking here: a cell belongs to exactly one region.
Searching a fixed word in 8 directions (P1101) and chaining words by overlaps (P1019) are DFS with a different "move" step.

Breadth-first search (BFS) explores in layers: first every cell 1 step away, then every cell 2 steps away, and so on. The first time a cell is reached is therefore by a shortest path, when every move costs 1.
Use a queue (first in, first out): take the front cell, push its unvisited neighbours with distance + 1. Mark a cell as visited when you push it, so it is never queued twice.

dist[][] = -1 doubles as the "visited" mark. queue<pair<int, int>> stores a cell as two numbers; q.front().first and .second read them. Each cell enters the queue once, so the whole BFS is O(n × m) (P1443). left << setw(5) prints each number left-aligned in 5 columns.
BFS works on any states joined by moves of cost 1, not just grid cells. Here a state is a floor and the two buttons are the moves (P1135).

The same idea finds the fewest rule applications turning one string into another, with map<string, int> as the distance table (P1032); time steps (P2895) and teleporters (P1825) only change which moves exist.

Cells inside a closed loop are exactly the 0s that cannot be reached from outside. So flood the outside instead: start from the border and mark every reachable 0; whatever 0 is left unmarked is inside (P1162).
A padding ring of 0s around the grid joins all border cells into one region, so one BFS start at (0, 0) covers the whole outside.

title: 线性表
summary: Arrays and vectors, stacks, queues and linked lists: four ways to keep items in a row, each cheap for different operations.

boxes.text: A linear list keeps items in a row, each with one item before it and one after. The four structures of this chapter store such a row differently, and each makes different operations cheap. Choose by the operations the problem needs most.
105 lockers with up to 105 slots each would need 1010 boxes, but only q of them are ever used. A map stores only the used (key, value) pairs, each lookup costs O(log q) (P3613).
map[key] creates the key with value 0 if it is missing; that is exactly "empty slot" here. Use map.count(key) when you must not create it.
A stack is last in, first out (LIFO): you only touch the top, like a pile of plates. push puts on top, pop removes the top, top reads it; all O(1).
Use a stack when the most recent unfinished thing must be dealt with first: matching brackets, evaluating expressions, undoing steps, and turning recursion into a loop.

In postfix (后缀) notation the operator comes after its two operands, so no brackets are needed. Push numbers; on an operator, pop two, combine, push the result. The last value on the stack is the answer (P1449).
The first pop is the right operand. For - and / the order matters: 5 2 − means 5 − 2.

Brackets: each closer must match the most recent unmatched opener, which is the stack top; at the end nothing may be left (P1241 adds rules for repairing). Stack sequences: simulate with a real stack, popping whenever the top is the next value to pop; if anything is left, the order was impossible (P4387).
A queue is first in, first out (FIFO), like a line at a counter. push joins at the back, pop leaves from the front, front reads the first; all O(1).
BFS (第14章) is a queue. deque allows push and pop at both ends, useful for sliding windows such as "ships in the last 24 hours" (P2058).

A circle of people counting off becomes a queue: moving the front to the back is "pass to the next person" (P1996). A memory that forgets the oldest item is a queue plus a marking array that answers "is it stored?" in O(1) (P1540).

A linked list stores, for every item, who comes next (and, doubly linked, who comes before). Inserting or deleting only rewires a few links: O(1), with no shifting. The price: reaching the i-th item means walking from the head, O(n).
In contests, keep the links in two arrays, L[x] and R[x] , indexed by the item itself; node 0 is a fixed head that is never deleted, so the first item needs no special case.

"Insert left of k" is "insert right of k's left neighbour", so one insert function is enough. Delete by linking the two neighbours to each other. Walking R[] from the head prints the final order (P1160).
Rewire in the right order: read R[k] into x's links before overwriting R[k] .
For "closest earlier value" questions such as daily turnover (P2234), a sorted set with lower_bound gives each answer in O(log n) (集合 , 第17章).

title: 二叉树
summary: Binary trees: storing them, the four traversal orders, rebuilding a tree from two orders, search trees and distances.

boxes.text: A binary tree starts at one root; every node has at most two children, a left and a right. Nodes without children are leaves (green). The depth of a node counts the levels from the root; the tree's depth is the deepest level.
A complete binary tree fills every level from left to right, so it fits in an array with no pointers: root at 1, children of i at 2i and 2i + 1, parent at i / 2.

A knockout bracket is a complete binary tree: countries are leaves, every match is an internal node holding its winner. Fill the nodes from the bottom up; the runner-up is the loser of the final, the weaker of nodes 2 and 3 (P4715).

For a general tree, store each node's children in two arrays lc[u] and rc[u] , with 0 (or a symbol such as '*' ) for "none". Depth is recursive: an empty tree has depth 0, otherwise 1 + the deeper subtree (P4913).
The three depth-first orders differ only in when the root is printed: before, between or after its two subtrees. Each is a three-line recursive function.

Pre-order gives the root first, post-order gives it last; the root's position in the in-order splits the remaining letters into the left and right subtrees, and their sizes split the other order the same way.

Pre-order and post-order without in-order do not fix the tree: a node with only one child could have it on the left or the right. Such a node shows up as a pair "x y" in pre-order that appears as "y x" in post-order; each one doubles the count (P1229).

In a binary search tree (BST) every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger. Searching or inserting walks one path from the root: left if smaller, right if larger.
Inserting already sorted values makes the tree a long chain, and every operation becomes O(n). The library set keeps itself balanced (第17章); write your own BST to learn the idea.
Rank, k-th smallest, predecessor and successor are all one walk down the tree once each node also stores its subtree size (P5076).

Walking from a child back to its parent is allowed here, so treat the tree as an undirected graph: store every edge in both directions with vector<int> adj[N] . With n ≤ 100, run a BFS from every node and keep the cheapest total (P1364).

Depth, width (the most nodes on one level) and the distance between two nodes (up to their lowest common ancestor and down again) come from one BFS that records depth and parent (P3884). Drawing a tree in text (P1185) places each node by its depth and in-order position.

title: 集合
summary: Union-find for merging groups, hashing for fast lookup, and set/map for sorted collections.

boxes.text: Union-find (并查集 , disjoint set union) keeps items split into groups and answers two questions fast: find "which group is x in?" and union "merge the groups of x and y". Each group is a tree stored in a parent[] array; the root represents the group.
Path compression: while finding the root, point every node on the way straight at the root. After that, operations are almost O(1) each.

Relatives are a union-find on people (P1551). To connect g separate groups you need exactly g − 1 more roads, and every successful union lowers g by one (P1536). Family trees with names use map<string, string> as the parent array (P2814).

"The enemy of my enemy is my friend": give each person i a second node i + n meaning "i's enemies", and unite a with b + n, b with a + n (P1892). Checking constraints in the right order, equalities first, uses the same tool after compressing big numbers (P1955).

A hash turns a key (a number, a string) into a small index, so the key can be stored in or looked up from an array slot directly. Different keys may land on the same index (a collision); a good hash makes that rare, and a hash table keeps a short list per slot.

Read the string as a number in base 131 and let unsigned long long overflow, which is arithmetic mod 264. Equal strings always get equal hashes; different strings almost never do. Then count distinct values with sort + unique (P3370).
A hash compares fingerprints, not the strings themselves: a collision gives a wrong answer silently. Use a large base and mod 264 (or two different hashes) to make it practically impossible.
Keep the first copy of each number: print it only if it was not seen before (P4305). Use the hash containers when order does not matter and speed does.

set keeps distinct values sorted; map keeps (key, value) pairs sorted by key. Besides insert, find and erase in O(log n), they answer "nearest value" questions with lower_bound , which a hash table cannot do.

lower_bound points at the first value ≥ len; the closest value is that one or the one just before it (prev(it) ), as in 第13章(P5250). map.erase(key) returns how many entries it removed, which answers "did it exist?" (P5266).

title: 图的基本应用
summary: Vertices and edges: storing a graph, searching it with DFS and BFS, and ordering a DAG topologically.

boxes.text: A graph is a set of vertices (points) joined by edges. Edges may be directed (one-way arrows) or undirected, and may carry a weight (a length or a cost). Trees, grids and "who depends on whom" are all graphs.
Store a graph as an adjacency list: vector<int> adj[N] , where adj[u] lists the vertices an edge from u reaches. Memory O(n + m). An undirected edge is stored twice, once in each direction.
DFS and BFS from 第14章 work on any graph: replace "the four neighbouring cells" by "every vertex in adj[u] ". A visited array stops the search from going round a cycle forever.

Sorting each adj[u] makes the search visit smaller numbers first, which is what "print in the required order" problems want (P5318). DFS is O(n + m): each vertex is entered once and each edge is looked at once.

"From each vertex, the largest vertex you can reach" is slow from every vertex separately. Turn it around: reverse every edge, then start from n, n − 1, … and label everything each one can reach that has no label yet (P3916).
Graph search can run out of stack on 105-long paths; if that happens, use BFS or an explicit stack instead of recursion.

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) has directed edges and no cycle. Its vertices can be lined up so every edge points forward: a topological order. Tasks with "must happen before" rules, food chains and course prerequisites are DAGs.

Kahn's algorithm: count each vertex's incoming edges (in-degree); queue every vertex with in-degree 0; pop one, output it, and remove its edges, queuing any vertex whose in-degree drops to 0. If fewer than n vertices come out, the graph has a cycle.

In topological order, every vertex is processed only after all vertices that point into it, so a recurrence over the DAG ("number of ways", "longest time") can be filled in that order, exactly like 第11章(P4017).

Start the topological order from every in-degree-0 vertex, not only from vertex 1: vertices that vertex 1 cannot reach still have to remove their edges, or their targets never reach in-degree 0. Keep "unreachable" as a separate value so it is never extended (P1807).
Chores with durations (P1113) are the same longest-path idea; deciding whether a set of "A < B" facts gives a unique order checks that the queue never holds two vertices at once (P1347).

title: 位运算与进制转换
summary: Number bases and conversion, how integers really sit in binary, and bit operators as logic on 32 facts at once.

boxes.text: In base b, each digit is worth b times the digit to its right: 1101 in base 2 is 1·8 + 1·4 + 0·2 + 1·1 = 13. Bases above 10 use letters for the extra digits: A = 10, B = 11, … , F = 15 in hexadecimal.
Base b → number: read digits from the left, value = value × b + digit. Number → base b: repeatedly take value % b as the next digit from the right and divide by b; reverse at the end.

Use do … while so that 0 prints as "0". A negative base works the same way, except that C++ may give a negative remainder: add |b| to the digit and 1 to the quotient, which keeps n = q·b + r true (P1017).

A computer stores an int as 32 bits. Non-negative values are plain binary. Negative values use two's complement: −x is stored as (232 − x), which is "flip every bit of x and add 1". That is why the top bit acts as a sign, and why int runs from −231 to 231 − 1.
Signed overflow (INT_MAX + 1 ) is undefined behaviour in C++, not a guaranteed wrap. Use unsigned when you want wrapping, as in hashing (第17章) and bit swaps (P1100).

A proposition is true or false, a bit is 1 or 0. The bit operators apply and / or / not / xor to all 32 bits at once, so one integer can hold 32 true/false facts, and one operation updates all of them.
Implication "p → q" is !p || q . De Morgan: ~(a & b) == (~a | ~b) and ~ (a | b) == (~a & ~b) .

XOR cancels pairs (a ^ a = 0 , a ^ 0 = a ) and does not care about order, so XOR-ing everything leaves the one value that appears an odd number of times, in O(1) memory (P1469). The subset masks of 第10章 are these same tricks: mask >> i & 1 tests bit i.
Enumerating masks 0 … 2k − 1 tries every true/false assignment of k propositions: the brute-force way to check a logic puzzle or prove two formulas equal.

title: 计数原理与排列组合
summary: Adding separate cases, multiplying independent steps, counting the complement, permutations, combinations and Pascal's triangle.

boxes.text: Addition principle (加法原理): if the ways split into separate cases with no overlap, add the counts of the cases. Multiplication principle (乘法原理): if a choice is made in independent steps, multiply the number of options at each step.

Draw the choices as a tree: a branching step multiplies, separate whole branches add. The usual trap is double counting (cases that overlap) or steps whose options depend on earlier choices; then count the dependent step after fixing the order.

Each rabbit picks a different number from 1 to its own maximum. Give numbers to the most limited rabbit first: when it is rabbit i's turn (0-based), exactly i numbers inside its range are already used, so it has max − i choices. Multiply (P1866).
Sorting makes each step's choices independent of which numbers were taken, only of how many. Take every product % MOD as you go.

Counting attacked cells directly double counts every cell that is hit by both a row and a column. Count the complement instead: a cell is safe exactly when its row has no rook and its column has no rook, (n − r)(n − c) cells by the multiplication principle (P3913).
"Count what you do not want, then subtract" avoids overlaps. Line intersections (P2789) split by how many lines are parallel, and adding up the cases is the addition principle.
A permutation counts ordered arrangements; a combination counts unordered selections. Each combination of k items can be ordered in k! ways, so P(n, k) = C(n, k) · k!.
Pascal's rule: either item n is chosen (then choose k − 1 of the rest) or it is not (choose k of the rest). Filling the triangle (第5章) needs only additions, so no division and no huge factorials.

Store C(i, j) mod k: "divisible by k" means the value mod k is 0, and Pascal's rule works mod k too. Up to 104 queries then read a 2D prefix sum in O(1) each instead of rescanning the triangle (P2822).

Only words with strictly increasing letters get a code, ordered by length and then alphabetically. Code of a word = 1 + (number of valid words before it): all shorter words, C(26, len) for each length, plus same- length words that are smaller at the first differing position (P1246).

After fixing a smaller letter ch at position i, the remaining L − i − 1 letters are any increasing choice from the 26 − ch letters above ch: C(26 − ch, L − i − 1). Stars-and-bars style splitting (P2638) is another "choose positions" count.

luogu.name: [NOIP 2016 提高组 ] 组合数问题

title: 整除理论
summary: Divisibility and remainders, primes and sieves, gcd and lcm, and the prime factorisation behind them all.

boxes.text: Divisibility is the heart of number theory problems. The mod rules let you keep numbers small: take % m after every addition and multiplication and the final remainder is still right. Division does not work this way.
Divisors pair up as d and n/d, so trying d up to √n finds them all (第4章). For "how many numbers in a list divide x" over many x, turn it around and walk the multiples of each value instead.

Walking multiples v, 2v, 3v, … for every v up to M costs M/1 + M/2 + … ≈ M ln M, fast for M = 106 (P2926). Counting divisors of every number 1 … n by "how many multiples does i have" turns into Σ ⌊n / i⌋ (P1403).
A prime has exactly two divisors, 1 and itself; other numbers above 1 are composite. Testing one number takes O(√n). To find all primes up to N, sieve: for each prime p, cross out its multiples.
Linear sieve (欧拉筛): cross out each composite exactly once, by its smallest prime factor; O(N). It also gives every number's smallest prime factor for free.

vector<bool> stores one bit per entry, so 108 flags fit in about 12 MB (P3383). A huge range [L, R] that is short (R − L ≤ 106) is sieved with only the primes up to √R, crossing out from the first multiple ≥ L: a segmented sieve (P1835). Remember that 1 is not prime.

The greatest common divisor gcd(a, b) is the largest number dividing both; the least common multiple lcm(a, b) is the smallest number both divide. Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), ending at gcd(a, 0) = a, in O(log). And gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b.

If gcd(P, Q) = x and lcm(P, Q) = y, then P = x·a and Q = x·b with a·b = y/x and gcd(a, b) = 1, so counting pairs means counting coprime splits of y/x (P1029). Write a / gcd(a, b) * b , dividing first, so the lcm does not overflow on the way (P4057). Reducing fractions (P1572) divides top and bottom by their gcd.
Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, n = p₁e₁ · p₂e₂ ⋯. Factor by trial division up to √n; whatever is left above 1 is one last prime.

A divisor of n picks each exponent from 0 to eᵢ independently, so the multiplication principle (第20章) gives Π(eᵢ + 1) divisors: 360 = 2³·3²·5 has 4·3·2 = 24. "How long until cells divide evenly into tubes" compares exponents of the same primes (P1069); the divisor sum of ab mod 9901 uses the sum formula with fast powers (P1593).

title: 常见优化技巧
summary: Turn O(n²) scans into O(n): two pointers, storing results instead of recomputing, monotonic stacks and monotonic queues.

boxes.text: Two pointers (双指针): keep a window [l, r] and move both ends only forward.

Same-direction pointers handle "shortest / longest window with a property". Opposite-direction pointers (one at each end of a sorted array, moving inward) handle "pairs with a given sum or difference".

For each right end r, the shortest good window ends at r and starts at the largest l that still keeps every painter. That l never moves back when r grows, so l and r together move at most 2n times (P1638). Keep a cnt[] array and a kinds counter so each step is O(1).

Longest window without repeats (UVA11572) shrinks only when the new value is already inside. Counting pairs with a − b = c (P1102) after sorting: as a[i] grows, the block of values equal to a[i] + c only moves right, so two pointers replace the binary searches of 第13章 . Diamond Collector (P3143) and Sure Bet (P4653) are two-pointer scans on sorted data.

Space for time (空间换时间): store results you would otherwise recompute, such as a running total, a prefix minimum or a count per value, so each step reads them in O(1). The cost is memory, which is usually plentiful compared with time.

Checking all O(n²) subarrays is too slow for n = 2 × 10⁵. Keep only one stored value: the best sum of a subarray ending at the current position. It either extends the previous best or starts fresh, whichever is larger (P1115).
The same answer comes from prefix sums: best = max over r of (S[r] − min S[l] for l < r), with the minimum stored as you go. One stored number replaces a whole inner loop.

Re-sorting after every new score costs O(n log n) each time. Scores are only 0 … 600, so store a count per score and walk down from 600 until enough winners are covered: at most 601 steps per player (P7072).

When values come from a small range, a counting array (基础篇第5章) is the "space" that buys the time. Grouping indices by colour and parity before pairing them up (P2671) is the same idea with sums stored per group.

A monotonic stack (单调栈) keeps its contents sorted, for example decreasing from bottom to top. Before pushing x, pop everything that x "beats". Each element is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n) in total.
At the moment an element is popped, the element causing the pop is its next greater (or smaller) element to the right. What remains below it in the stack is its nearest greater element to the left.

Count, for every cow, how many cows to its right it can see over. Turn it around: when cow i arrives, the cows that can see it are exactly the taller ones still in a decreasing stack. Shorter or equal ones are popped forever, since cow i blocks their view (P2866).

Largest rectangle of F cells: for every row, h[j] is how many F cells stand in column j ending at this row. The best rectangle with height h[j] stretches left and right until the first lower column, found for all j with two monotonic-stack passes: O(nm) overall (P4147). Counting all rectangles (P1950) and the poster problem (P3467) use the same "nearest lower" arrays.

A monotonic queue (单调队列) finds the minimum (or maximum) of every window of length k in O(n) total. Keep a deque of indices whose values increase from front to back: a new value pops every bigger value from the back, because those can never be a window minimum again; the front leaves when it falls out of the window.
The front of the deque is always the minimum of the current window. Each index enters and leaves once.

Best sum of at most m consecutive pieces: with prefix sums, the sum of (l, r] is S[r] − S[l], so for each r we want the smallest S[l] with r − m ≤ l < r: a sliding-window minimum over the prefix sums (P1714).

Window maximum (P2032), the max − min of every k × k square by running the queue on rows and then on columns (P2216), and recurrences like "best of the last k states" (P1725) all reuse this deque. Range max/min with arbitrary queries (P2880) needs a sparse table (第3章).

title: 前缀和、差分与离散化
summary: O(1) range sums, O(1) range updates, and shrinking huge coordinates to their ranks.

boxes.text: Prefix sums (前缀和): S[i] = a[1] + … + a[i], with S[0] = 0. Building S takes one pass; then the sum of any range a[l..r] is S[r] − S[l − 1] in O(1), instead of O(r − l) by adding.
Use 1-based indexing so that S[0] = 0 exists and l = 1 needs no special case.
With m queries on n numbers, adding each range costs O(nm); prefix sums cost O(n + m). This is the first tool to try whenever a problem asks for many range sums (P8218).
The corner S[i−1][j−1] is counted twice when adding the strip above and the strip to the left, so subtract it once. In a query, the corner is subtracted twice, so add it back.

Maximum-sum rectangle: fix the top and bottom rows (O(n²) pairs); the column sums between them form a 1D array, and the best range of columns is the maximum subarray of 第1章 . Column prefix sums give each value in O(1): O(n³) in total (P1719).
Binary search on a parameter, with prefix sums so that each check is O(n), solves the quality inspector (P1314); splitting brownies into an even grid checks each guess with 2D prefix sums (P3017).

Difference array (差分): d[i] = a[i] − a[i − 1]. Adding v to a whole range a[l..r] changes only two entries: d[l] += v, d[r + 1] −= v. After all updates, a prefix sum over d rebuilds a. Range updates become O(1) each.
Prefix sums and differences undo each other: prefix sums answer many range queries, differences apply many range updates. Use differences when all updates come before all queries.

Changing a range by ±1 changes one difference up and one down (or one at the ends). To make all values equal, every d[2..n] must become 0: pair a positive with a negative while both exist, then fix the rest alone, so the answer is max(pos, neg) operations (P4552). Ticket counting per rail segment (P3406) and checking orders for classrooms with binary search (P1083) are difference arrays too.

Adding 1 to a rectangle touches four corners of the 2D difference array. A 2D prefix sum afterwards turns the corners back into the full counts: O(1) per carpet and O(n²) once at the end, instead of O(n²) per carpet (P3397).
Flipping k cows at a time with as few flips as possible keeps a running difference of "flips still active" while scanning (P2882).

Discretisation (离散化): when only the order of values matters, not their size, replace each value by its rank among the distinct values. Coordinates up to 109 become 0 … n − 1, small enough to index an array.
Recipe: copy the values, sort , unique + erase , then rank(x) = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) - v.begin() . O(n log n).

The sorted endpoints cut the line into at most 2n pieces; inside one piece nothing changes. A difference array over the piece numbers counts how many intervals cover each piece, and covered pieces add their real length xs[i + 1] − xs[i] (P1496).

In 2D, the sorted x and y coordinates cut the plane into at most 2n × 2n cells; a 2D difference marks which cells are covered and each covered cell adds its real area (P1884). Program analysis with huge variable numbers discretises before union-find (P1955); skylines (P1904), cow line-ups (P3029) and parity games (P5937) compress coordinates the same way.
After discretising, distance is lost: ranks 3 and 4 may be far apart in reality. Always add back the real length (xs[i + 1] − xs[i] ) when measuring, and keep both ends of every interval in the list.

title: 分治与倍增
summary: Split into halves and combine; precompute blocks of length 2ᵏ and jump by powers of two.

boxes.text: Divide and conquer (分治): split the problem into halves, solve each half recursively, then combine the two answers. If combining costs O(n), the whole thing costs O(n log n): there are log n levels, each doing O(n) work.
Merge sort is the model: sort both halves, then merge two sorted lists. Anything that can be counted while merging, such as inversions, comes for free.

When a[j] from the right half is placed before a[i] from the left half, it is smaller than every remaining a[i..m]: that is m − i + 1 inversions at once (P1908). Use long long : n = 5 × 10⁵ can give 1.25 × 10¹¹ inversions. Two rows of matches need as many adjacent swaps as there are inversions after matching ranks (P1966).
ab by multiplying b times is O(b), hopeless for b = 10⁹. Write b in binary: ab is the product of a2ᵏ over the 1-bits of b, and a2ᵏ comes from squaring. O(log b) multiplications (P1226).

Take % p after every multiplication, and keep values in long long so a product of two numbers below p (up to about 3 × 10⁹) fits. Start from 1 % p , so p = 1 gives 0. With big numbers instead of mod, the same loop computes 2ᴾ (P1045).

Many sequence problems split the same way: the answer lies entirely in the left half, entirely in the right half, or crosses the middle. Recursion handles the first two; only the crossing case needs new code, and it usually has a simple shape because it must touch the middle.

A crossing subarray = (best sum ending at m, going left) + (best sum starting at m + 1, going right). Two linear scans per level: O(n log n). The O(n) method of 第1章 is faster, but this pattern carries over to problems that have no simple scan (P1115).

Closest pair of points: after solving both halves with best distance d, a crossing pair must lie within d of the dividing line, and sorted by y each point only needs to be compared with the next few points closer than d vertically: O(n log² n) (P1257). Sums over all pairs such as MooFest (P2345) are also counted across the middle while merging.

Binary lifting (倍增): precompute the answer for blocks of length 1, 2, 4, 8, …; any length is a sum of powers of two, so a few precomputed blocks cover it. A sparse table (ST 表) stores mx[k][i] = max of a[i … i + 2ᵏ − 1].

A range max/min query [l, r] is covered by two overlapping blocks of length 2ᵏ, with k = ⌊log₂(r − l + 1)⌋: one starting at l, one ending at r. Overlap is harmless for max and min, so each query is O(1) after O(n log n) preparation.

A block of length 2ᵏ is two blocks of length 2ᵏ⁻¹, so each table row comes from the row before. The tallest minus the shortest cow in a range (P2880) and the most loyal (smallest) account in a range (P1816) are direct ST-table queries. Sums do not work with overlapping blocks; use prefix sums for those.

When every position has exactly one "next" position, 2ᵏ steps = two jumps of 2ᵏ⁻¹ steps. With the table, t steps (even t = 10¹²) take one jump per 1-bit of t: O(log t) per query, the same binary idea as fast power.

Water falling through fountains (P7167), the fewest guards to cover a circle (P4155) and frogs jumping k times (P3509) all build such a jump table and then jump by powers of two. In 第9章 the same table finds lowest common ancestors in trees.

title: 进阶搜索
summary: Make search fast: prune branches, deepen step by step, meet in the middle, and let a heuristic point the way.

boxes.text: A plain DFS (基础篇第14章) visits every branch. Pruning (剪枝) proves early that a branch cannot lead to a (better) answer and cuts it off. Good pruning often turns "never finishes" into "a few milliseconds"; the answer stays the same.

Rebuilding broken sticks (P1120) needs every kind of cut: the original length divides the total; pieces are tried longest first and in increasing index (no reordering of the same stick); a failed length is not retried; if the first piece of a new stick fails, or a piece that exactly finishes a stick fails, no other choice can work, so the whole branch returns false.

Optimality pruning: once a full route of length best is known, any partial route already that long is abandoned. The better the first answer found, the more is cut, which is why visiting nearer pieces first can help (P1433).

For n up to 15 the safe method is a state over "which pieces are eaten" (状态压缩 , 第17章); pruning only makes plain DFS fast on typical data. Sudoku-like puzzles (P1074) fill the cell with the fewest options first.

Iterative deepening (迭代加深 , IDDFS): run a DFS that refuses to go deeper than D; if it fails, try D + 1. The first D that succeeds is the shallowest answer, like BFS, but memory stays as small as DFS. The repeated shallow levels cost little because the deepest level dominates.
Use it when the answer is shallow but the tree is wide or infinite in depth: plain DFS would wander deep and never return, and BFS would need too much memory.

Shortest addition chain: start from 1, each new number is the sum of two earlier ones, reach n with the fewest additions. The depth is small (about 2 log₂ n) but every level has many choices, a perfect fit for iterative deepening.
The doubling test is an estimate of the steps still needed: even doubling every time cannot reach n, so stop. Egyptian fractions (P1763) use the same "deepen, estimate, cut" pattern.

240 subsets are far too many, but 2 × 220 ≈ 2 million half-subsets are fine. Meet in the middle (双向搜索 / 折半搜索): enumerate each half separately, sort one side, and count matching pairs with binary search (P4799).

The pattern works whenever the answer is "a choice from the left half combined with a choice from the right half": sums (CF525E with factorials), products below a bound (CF912E). Searching from both ends of a graph toward each other is the same idea.

Heuristic search (启发式搜索) uses an estimate h(state) of the remaining cost to explore promising states first. A*: always expand the state with the smallest f = g + h, where g is the cost so far. If h never overestimates the true remaining cost, the first time the goal is taken from the queue its cost is optimal.

A good h is cheap to compute and as close to the truth as possible without exceeding it. For sliding puzzles, "how many tiles are out of place" and "total Manhattan distance of the tiles" both never overestimate.

The board is a 9-character string, the queue is ordered by g + h, and map<string, int> keeps the best known cost of every state (P1379). Plain BFS explores states in every direction; A* heads toward the goal.
An h that sometimes overestimates can make A* return a non-optimal answer. When unsure, take a weaker estimate; h = 0 turns A* back into ordinary shortest-path search.

title: 二叉堆与树状数组
summary: Heaps for the smallest (or largest) element in O(log n), and Fenwick trees for prefix sums that can change.

boxes.text: A binary heap (二叉堆) is a complete binary tree stored in an array (children of i at 2i and 2i + 1, 基础篇第16章) with one rule: every parent ≤ its children. The minimum is always at h[1]. Insert and delete-min each walk one root-to-leaf path: O(log n).
Insert: put the value at the end, then sift up (swap with the parent while smaller). Delete-min: move the last value to the root, then sift down (swap with the smaller child while larger).
The tree has height log₂ n, so sift up and sift down each take O(log n) swaps; reading the minimum is O(1) (P3378). Building a heap from n values by sifting down from n/2 to 1 is even O(n).

C++ already has a heap: priority_queue<T> keeps the largest on top; priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T>> keeps the smallest. push , pop O(log n), top O(1). Pairs compare by the first field, then the second.

Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, with sizes equal or the small half one bigger. The median is then the top of the small half (P1168). The same two-heap split answers "the k- th smallest so far" with a moving k (P1801).

The n smallest of all n² sums: row i is sorted, so only the next unused element of each row can be next; a heap of n "row fronts" gives each answer in O(log n) (P1631, also P2085). Deadlines: take jobs by deadline, and when time runs out drop the longest job taken so far, found in O(log n) with a max-heap (P4053).

Huffman with k-ary trees (P2168) adds zero-weight leaves so that every merge takes exactly k; earthworms (P2827) replace the heap by three queues that stay sorted on their own; dancing pairs (P1878) keep candidate adjacent pairs in a heap and skip stale ones.

A Fenwick tree (树状数组 , BIT) stores t[i] = sum of a over the block (i − lowbit(i), i], where lowbit(i) = i & −i is the lowest set bit. A prefix sum adds about log n blocks, jumping i −= lowbit(i); a point update changes about log n blocks, jumping i += lowbit(i).
Prefix sums (进阶篇第2章) answer queries in O(1) but cannot change; a Fenwick tree does both query and update in O(log n), with a 10-line implementation.
Point update + range sum (P3374) is the basic form. Store the difference array instead and the same tree does range add + point query (P3368), the 第2章 trick made dynamic.

Inversions again (P1908, also 第3章 by merge sort): scan left to right, and before inserting a[i] ask how many earlier values are ≤ a[i]; the rest of the i earlier values are larger. Discretise first so the values index the tree.

Equal values are not inversions: count earlier values ≤ a[i] (not <), as above. Matching match-sticks (P1966), counting close pairs (P5677) and booking a hall (P2161) all reduce to counting with a Fenwick tree.

title: 线段树
summary: One tree over ranges for sums, maxima and anything mergeable, with lazy tags for range updates, and a value tree for order statistics.

boxes.text: A segment tree (线段树) splits [1, n] into halves again and again; every node stores a summary (sum, max, …) of its range. Node p has children 2p and 2p + 1, like a heap. Any range [l, r] is covered by O(log n) nodes (green: [1, 4] = [1, 3] + [4, 4]), so queries and updates cost O(log n).
Unlike prefix sums and Fenwick trees, a segment tree can store anything that two halves can be combined into: sums, max/min, max subarray, counts of colours. Allocate 4n nodes.
Every update and query follows the same three cases: node range outside [x, y] → ignore; fully inside → use or mark this node; otherwise → push down, recurse into both halves, push up.
Push down before going into the children, in both update and query, or children answer with stale values. Sums reach 10¹⁸: use long long for sums and tags.

This is the template for range add + range sum (P3372). Range max/min only changes pushup (max instead of +) and what a tag does to a node (P1816). Flipping lights on a range keeps the count of lit lights and a "flip" tag that toggles (P3870).

Two kinds of tags at once need an order. For "multiply then add", store each node's pending change as x → x · mul + add. A new multiply c turns it into x · (mul·c) + add·c; a new add c turns it into x · mul + (add + c). Push both down together.

Writing every pending change as the same shape (x · mul + add) makes combining two changes a small formula, so any order of operations is handled by one apply (P3373). "Set to v" plus "add v" (P1253) works the same way with an "assigned?" flag that clears the add.

The best subarray of a range lies in the left half, in the right half, or crosses the middle (进阶篇第3章). Each node keeps four numbers so that two halves can always be merged: total, best prefix, best suffix, best inside. Queries merge the O(log n) nodes they meet (P4513).

Variance (P1471) keeps Σx and Σx²; the longest alternating run (P6492) keeps run lengths at both ends; square roots on ranges (P4145) stop once a node's max is 1. Design the node first: "what must I know about each half to answer for the whole?"

A value segment tree (权值线段树) is built over values instead of positions: leaf v counts how many times v has appeared. It answers "how many seen values are ≤ x" and "what is the k-th smallest seen value" in O(log V); discretise first if values are large.

k-th smallest: walk down from the root; if the left child holds at least k values go left, otherwise subtract its count and go right. Counting increasing triples (P1637): fix the middle element; multiply "smaller values before it" by "larger values after it", both counts over values, so a value tree or the equivalent Fenwick tree (进阶篇第5章) does the job. Inversions (P1908) and point sets with "first point to the upper right" (CF19D) also count over values.
A value tree needs a leaf for every possible value. Values up to 10⁹ must be discretised (第2章) first, or the tree built dynamically, creating nodes only when they are reached.

title: 字符串
summary: Match a pattern without ever stepping back, read periods straight off the border array, and store many words, or many binary numbers, in one tree.

boxes.text: Find pattern p (length m) inside text s (length n). Brute force restarts after each mismatch: O(nm). KMP never moves backwards in s. It precomputes, for every prefix p[1..i], nxt[i] = the length of its longest border (前缀函数 / 失配数组): a proper prefix that is also a suffix.
On a mismatch after j matched characters, the last nxt[j] characters of s still match the first nxt[j] of p, so set j = nxt[j] and try again; no character of s is read twice. Total O(n + m).

Both loops are the same code: building nxt is "searching p in itself". The while-loop looks slow, but j rises by at most 1 per step and every fallback lowers it, so the total work is O(n + m) (P3375).

Use p[j + 1] with 1-based strings and remember j = nxt[j] after a full match, otherwise overlapping matches (ABA in ABABA) are lost. Compare j with m, not with the string's size after adding the padding space.

If a string has a border of length b, shifting it by n − b lines it up with itself, so n − b is a period. The longest border nxt[n] gives the shortest period n − nxt[n] (P4391: "cabcabca" is a cut of "cab" repeated).
The string is an exact repetition of its shortest period only when n % (n − nxt[n]) == 0. Following nxt[n], nxt[nxt[n]], … lists every border from longest to shortest.
The shortest non-empty border is the last stop on the chain i → nxt[i] → nxt[nxt[i]] → …. Walking the chain each time can be slow, so store it: shortest[i] copies shortest[nxt[i]] (P3435).
Counting borders with extra conditions (P2375 动物园 : borders no longer than half) also walks the nxt chain, with a second pointer that never grows past i / 2.
A trie (字典树) stores a set of strings as paths from the root, one edge per letter.

Insert and look-up both walk the word letter by letter: O(length), independent of how many words are stored. Mark the node where a word ends, otherwise "ad" would wrongly count "a" as present when only "ad" was inserted.

The array size is the total number of letters inserted plus one, not the number of words. Each node keeps whatever the problem needs: an end mark, a counter, a "visited" state (P2580). set<string> would also work here, but the trie also answers prefix questions.

Prefix questions are natural on a trie: the words that are prefixes of w are exactly the word-ends on w's path. The longest chain "each word is a prefix of the next" ends at some word, and has as many words as there are word-ends on its path: i → in → int → intern → internet (P1481).
Count in the other direction too: store how many words pass through each node, and "how many words start with this prefix" is one look-up (P2922 Secret Message uses both counts).

Write numbers in binary from the highest bit and insert them into a trie with two letters, 0 and 1. To find the stored y that makes x xor y largest, walk from the top bit and take the opposite bit whenever that child exists: a 1 in a higher bit beats everything below it.
Insert all numbers, then query each one: the largest xor of a pair in O(n · 31). The greedy is right because bit k is worth more than bits 0 … k − 1 together.

The xor of the path u → v equals dis[u] xor dis[v], where dis is the xor from the root: the shared part above their meeting point cancels (x xor x = 0). So "longest xor path in a tree" becomes "largest xor of two numbers" (P4551).

Size the 0-1 trie as (number of values) × (bits) + 1 nodes. A persistent 0-1 trie answers the same question inside a range of the array (P4735, P4592); the k largest pair xors use a heap on top (P5283).
