title: 网络流与字符串补充
en: ISAP, mixed Euler circuits, endpos, suffix trees
summary: Run max flow with one BFS and relabelling (ISAP), decide Euler circuits in mixed graphs with a flow, and connect endpos classes, suffix trees, suffix arrays and suffix automata.

boxes.text: ISAP (Improved Shortest Augmenting Path) keeps a distance label d[v] = distance from v to the sink in the residual graph, computed once by BFS from t. It only pushes along edges with d[u] = d[v] + 1; when u has no such edge, it relabels d[u] to 1 + the smallest label among its usable neighbours, instead of rebuilding all levels as Dinic does.

Gap optimisation: keep cnt[k] = number of vertices with label k. If relabelling empties some cnt[k], no path from s to t can exist any more, so stop. With current-arc and gap, ISAP is usually as fast as or faster than Dinic, and needs only one BFS.

The first test is the sample of 第1章(50); the second is a random graph checked against a separate Edmonds–Karp in Python (BFS shortest augmenting paths, the simplest correct max-flow method). Ford– Fulkerson = any augmenting path; Edmonds–Karp = shortest by BFS, O(nm²); Dinic and ISAP = layered, O(n²m).

Euler circuit in a mixed graph (混合图的欧拉回路): some edges are directed, others may be oriented either way. Orient the undirected edges arbitrarily and compute xv = out(v) − in(v). Every xv must be even (flipping an edge changes it by 2). Then decide which undirected edges to flip with a flow: flipping u → v moves 2 from xu to xv.

Build: each undirected edge oriented u → v gives a flow edge u → v of capacity 1 (flipping it); s → v with capacity xv/2 for xv > 0, v → t with capacity −xv/2 for xv < 0. A circuit exists iff the flow saturates all source edges (and the edges are connected). Bridges (P3511) binary-searches a limit and runs this test.

Three small mixed graphs (all connected), checked against trying every orientation of the undirected edges in Python. Connectivity of the edges must be checked separately, as for ordinary Euler circuits (第17章).

endpos and equivalence classes: endpos(t) = the set of positions where substring t ends in s. Substrings with the same endpos form one class, and each class is one state of the suffix automaton (第3章). Within a class the strings are suffixes of each other with consecutive lengths len[link[v]] + 1 … len[v]; a shorter suffix has a larger (or equal) endpos set, which is why suffix links point to the next larger set and form a tree.
The number of occurrences of a state = |endpos| = the number of prefix-end states in its link subtree; that is the counting used in 第3章 's sam.cpp.

A suffix tree (后缀树) is the trie of all suffixes of s$ with every chain of single-child nodes compressed into one edge labelled by a substring: at most 2n nodes. Each leaf is a suffix; the path label of an internal node is a substring that repeats.

Three structures, one object: the suffix tree of s is the link tree of the suffix automaton of reversed s; its leaves read in lexicographic edge order give the suffix array, and the string depth of the LCA of two leaves is their LCP (height). In contests the suffix array or SAM replaces an explicit suffix tree (Ukkonen's construction is long and error-prone).

title: 上下界网络流
summary: Force every lower bound first, repair the imbalance with a super source and sink, and then push the flow up or down for the maximum or minimum feasible s–t flow.

boxes.text: Flows with lower bounds (上下界网络流): every edge needs low ≤ f ≤ high. Force the minimum first: send low on every edge unconditionally. That leaves an imbalance at the vertices: ex[v] = (lows coming in) − (lows going out). Keep the edge with capacity high − low for the free part, and fix the imbalance with a new super source S' → v (capacity ex[v] > 0) and v → super sink T' (capacity −ex[v]).

Feasible circulation (无源汇): feasible iff max flow S' → T' saturates every S' edge. With source s and sink t (有源汇): first add t → s with capacity ∞, so the s–t flow can circulate; check feasibility the same way; the flow on t → s is then one feasible flow value f₀.

Prints the maximum and minimum s–t flow, or that none is feasible. All three tests are checked in Python by trying every flow value on every edge (they are small on purpose); the second network is infeasible because 2–3 needs at least 2 but 1–2 can bring at most 1.
Removing t → s means zeroing both directions of that edge pair before the second max flow; otherwise the flow just runs around it. The super source and sink must not be confused with s and t.

title: 最小树形图与斯坦纳树
summary: The cheapest directed spanning tree by contracting cycles of cheapest incoming edges, and the cheapest tree connecting chosen terminals by subset DP plus Dijkstra.

boxes.text: A minimum arborescence (最小树形图) is the cheapest set of directed edges in which every vertex except the root r has exactly one incoming edge and all vertices are reachable from r. Chu–Liu / Edmonds: give each vertex its cheapest incoming edge. If those edges form no cycle, done. Otherwise contract each cycle into one vertex, and for an edge (u, v) entering the cycle at v, reduce its weight by in[v] (choosing it means dropping v's old incoming edge). Repeat. O(nm) (P4716).

If some vertex has no incoming edge at all, there is no arborescence. The weights of the chosen cheapest edges are added to the answer before each contraction; the reduced weights pay the difference later.
A random graph checked against trying every choice of one incoming edge per vertex in Python; the second graph has no edge into vertex 3, so −1.

The minimum Steiner tree (最小斯坦纳树): connect k chosen terminal vertices at the lowest total edge weight, using any other vertices as helpers. NP-hard in general, but fine for small k: f[S][v] = cheapest tree that connects the terminal set S and contains v.

Two transitions: merge at v: f[S][v] = min over T ⊂ S of f[T][v] + f[S∖T][v] (O(3k n) over all S); move v along edges: for a fixed S, f[S][·] relaxes like Dijkstra (O(2k m log m)). Answer f[all][any terminal] (P6192).

Checked against trying every subset of the 9 edges in Python. The merge loop over subsets of S is the 3ᵏ part (拓展篇第12章); the Dijkstra part is needed because the cheapest tree may run through non-terminal helpers.

title: 一般图最大匹配
summary: Find augmenting paths in graphs with odd cycles by contracting each odd cycle into a blossom during the search.

boxes.text: In a general graph (一般图 , not bipartite) augmenting paths still decide maximum matching (Berge), but searching for them breaks on odd cycles: the alternating search can reach a vertex by paths of both parities. Edmonds' blossom algorithm (带花树) contracts such an odd cycle (a "blossom") into one vertex, keeps searching, and expands it when an augmenting path is found. O(n³) (P6113).

BFS from a free vertex, colouring vertices "outer" and "inner" alternately. An edge between two outer vertices closes a blossom: find their LCA in the search forest, and merge the cycle into one base vertex with DSU; inner vertices of the blossom become outer and join the queue. Reaching a free vertex from an outer one = augment along the stored pairs.
Four random graphs and a 5-cycle (whose answer is 2, the classic case where plain alternating search fails), each checked by exhaustive search over matchings in Python.
The lca walk must jump by pre[match[x]] (two steps of the alternating path) and compare bases; forgetting find() there produces wrong blossoms that only show up on graphs with nested odd cycles.

Tutte matrix (Tutte 矩阵): for an undirected graph build an n × n matrix with A[u][v] = xuv and A[v][u] = −xuv for every edge, 0 elsewhere. Tutte's theorem: its rank is twice the maximum matching size (as a matrix of symbols). Fill the symbols with random numbers modulo a large prime and the rank is correct with high probability (Schwartz–Zippel).

This gives the matching size with one Gaussian elimination, O(n³), and about 30 lines, much shorter than blossom. Finding the matching itself is possible with more linear algebra but blossom (above) is the usual tool for that.

Checked against an exact bitmask search for the maximum matching in Python. A wrong answer is possible only if the random values hit a root of the determinant polynomial: probability about n / 10⁹ per run; run twice with different seeds if in doubt.

title: 支配树
summary: Find, for every vertex, which vertices every path from the source must pass through: the DAG version by LCA and the general Lengauer–Tarjan algorithm.

boxes.text: In a directed graph with start vertex 1, vertex d dominates u if every path from 1 to u passes through d. Every reachable u ≠ 1 has an immediate dominator idom(u), the closest strict dominator, and the edges idom(u) → u form the dominator tree (支配树): d dominates u exactly when d is an ancestor of u in it.

Uses: "which single vertex removal cuts u off from the source" (灾难 P2597 on a food DAG), critical points in control-flow graphs. On a DAG, process vertices in topological order: idom(u) = LCA in the tree built so far of all u's predecessors. General graphs need Lengauer–Tarjan (below), O(m α(m)).

Lengauer–Tarjan: number vertices by DFS order. The semidominator sdom(w) = the smallest- numbered v from which a path reaches w using only vertices numbered above w in between. Compute sdom in reverse DFS order with a DSU-with-minimum ("eval"); then idom(w) = sdom(w) if the vertex with minimum sdom on the tree path sdom(w) → w is w itself, otherwise idom(w) = idom of that vertex.
For every vertex: how many vertices it dominates, itself included (P5180). Checked in Python by deleting each vertex and testing which vertices become unreachable from 1, the definition itself.
Compare semidominators by their DFS numbers, not by vertex labels. Unreachable vertices have no dominator; skip them as predecessors and print 0 for them.

title: 数据结构进阶
en: Tree chairman trees, segment tree beats, long-path decomposition, leftist heaps
summary: Path k-th smallest with persistent trees on root paths, range chmin with sums by keeping the top two values, and depth-indexed tree DP in O(n) by reusing the long child's memory.

boxes.text: Persistent segment trees on a tree (树上主席树): give every vertex the value tree of its whole root path, built from its parent's version plus its own value (进阶篇第8章 did the same along an array). Then the multiset of values on the path u–v is version(u) + version(v) − version(lca) − version(parent(lca)), and the k-th smallest is found by walking those four trees together (Count on a tree, P2633).
Memory n log n nodes; each query O(log n) after an LCA. Forests that merge (森林 P3302) rebuild the smaller tree's versions on top of the other one (small-to-large).

Random tree and path queries, checked against listing the path's values and sorting them in Python. Subtracting version(lca) and version(parent(lca)) removes the shared root part but keeps the LCA itself exactly once.

Segment tree beats (吉司机线段树) supports the "range chmin" update ai = min(ai, x) together with range sums. Each node stores the maximum mx, the strict second maximum se, and how many times the maximum occurs, cnt. For an update with x: if x ≥ mx, nothing changes; if se < x < mx, only the maximums change, so sum −= cnt·(mx − x) and mx = x right here (a lazy tag); otherwise recurse into the children.

The "otherwise" case looks slow, but it merges the two largest distinct values of the node, which can only happen O(log n) times per value: amortised O((n + q) log n) for chmin with sums. Historic maxima (CPU 监控 P4314, P6242) add more tags on the same idea.
Random chmin, sum and max operations checked against a plain array in Python. The push uses the parent's mx as a "chmin tag": a child can only be above it in its maximum.

Long-path decomposition (长链剖分): like heavy-light, but the "long" child is the one with the deepest subtree. For DP indexed by depth (f[u][j] = number of vertices j levels below u), the long child's array can be reused by shifting it one place (f[u][j + 1] = f[long][j]) with a shared memory pool, and only short children are merged element by element.

Every vertex is the top of exactly one long chain, and a short child's array has length = its chain length, so all merges together cost O(n). Uses: depth-indexed tree DP (CF1009F Dominant Indices), k-th ancestor in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing (P5903).
For every vertex: the smallest depth j (below it) with the most vertices at that depth in its subtree. Checked in Python by walking each subtree layer by layer.

Ties matter: when the long child's best depth ties with a smaller depth, the smaller one must win. Here a full tie (every depth has one vertex) resets the answer to 0, and short-chain merges prefer smaller j on equal counts.

A leftist heap (左偏树 , a mergeable heap 可并堆) is a binary heap-ordered tree where each node stores dist = length of the shortest path down to a missing child. The rule dist(left) ≥ dist(right) keeps the right spine O(log n) long, so two heaps merge in O(log n) by walking down right spines: keep the smaller root, merge its right child with the other heap, swap children if the rule breaks.

Push = merge with a one-node heap; pop = merge the two children of the root. Together with a DSU that maps each element to its heap root this solves "merge the heaps of x and y / delete the minimum of x's heap" (P3377). Its persistent version (copy nodes on the merge path) gives the fast k-th shortest path algorithm (NOI 篇第11章).

Random merges and delete-mins (ties broken by the smaller index, as in P3377), checked against plain Python sets. The deleted root keeps pointing to the new root, so path compression still finds the right heap for every element.

Edge divide and conquer (边分治): like centroid decomposition (点分治), but split the tree at the edge whose removal leaves the most balanced two parts. Every path through that edge is "a path in the left part ending at its end + the edge + a path in the right part", so each step combines exactly two sides, which is easier than merging many subtrees of a centroid.

A star breaks it (every edge leaves a part of size n − 1), so first binarise the tree: replace each vertex's children by a chain of virtual vertices joined by weight-0 edges. Degrees become ≤ 3 and the best edge always leaves parts of size ≥ about n/3, so the depth is O(log n). Virtual vertices are not counted. Used when the two-sided merge matters (P4220 通道 , and many "maximise f(path) over pairs" problems).
Counts pairs of real vertices at distance ≤ K, checked against all-pairs DFS in Python. Each pair is counted exactly once: at the first chosen edge that separates the two vertices.

title: Min_25 筛与 Powerful Number 筛
summary: Sum a multiplicative function up to 10¹⁰: first sum powers of primes over every ⌊n/i⌋ by sieving out smallest prime factors, then recurse over smallest prime factors for the composites.

boxes.text: Min_25 sieve (Min_25 筛) computes Σi≤n f(i) for a multiplicative f in about O(n3/4 / log n), for n up to 10¹⁰–10¹¹, provided f(p) is a low-degree polynomial in p and f(pk) is easy. Part 1: for every value v = ⌊n/i⌋ compute g(v) = Σp≤v, p prime pe by a sieve that removes, prime by prime, the numbers whose smallest prime factor is that prime.

Part 1 transition for the j-th prime pj (only for v ≥ pj²): g(v) −= pje · (g(⌊v/pj⌋) − g(pj−1)). There are only 2√n distinct values ⌊n/i⌋, stored in two arrays indexed by v (small) or n/v (large). Start from g(v) = Σ2≤i≤v ie, as if every number were prime.

Part 2: S(v, j) = Σ f(i) over 2 ≤ i ≤ v whose smallest prime factor is ≥ pj. It is (the prime part) g-values minus the primes below pj, plus, for each prime pk ≥ pj with pk² ≤ v and each power pke: f(pke)·S(⌊v/pke⌋, k + 1) + f(pke+1). Answer = S(n, 1) + f(1), computed by plain recursion without memo.
For φ: f(p) = p − 1, so part 1 needs two sums: primes counted (e = 0) and primes summed (e = 1); f(pk) = pk−1(p − 1). P5325 has f(pk) = pk(pk − 1), which needs e = 1 and e = 2.

Prints π(n) (from part 1) and Σφ(i) for i ≤ n (part 2), both checked against a plain sieve in Python up to 10⁶. The sum of primes below each prime is recomputed in a loop here for clarity; in real use keep it as a prefix-sum array.

The values in g overflow fast: Σ i up to 10¹⁰ is 5·10¹⁹, beyond long long. Real problems work modulo a prime; with exact sums, keep n small enough or use __int128. Precompute the prefix sums of primes, or the inner loop costs an extra factor.

The Powerful Number sieve (PN 筛) sums a multiplicative f up to n when some easy multiplicative g agrees with f on primes, g(p) = f(p), and its prefix sums G are known. Write f = g * h (Dirichlet convolution). Then h(p) = 0, so h is nonzero only on powerful numbers (every prime exponent ≥ 2), and there are only O(√n) of them up to n.

Σi≤n f(i) = Σd powerful h(d) · G(⌊n/d⌋). Find h(pk) from f(pk) = Σi=0..k g(pi) h(pk−i), then DFS over primes ≤ √n with exponents ≥ 2. Below, f(pk) = k·pk with g = id, so G(m) = m(m+1)/2. When G itself needs a sieve (杜教筛 or Min_25), PN wraps around it.
Checked against a direct sieve of f up to n in Python. The work is the number of powerful numbers, O(√n), plus the cost of G; for n = 10¹⁰ it runs in milliseconds.

title: 多项式进阶与 FWT
en: Polynomial inverse, ln, exp; bitwise convolution
summary: Invert, take logarithms and exponentials of power series with Newton iteration over NTT, and convolve by OR, AND and XOR with the fast Walsh transform.

boxes.text: Formal power series modulo xn and a prime (998244353) can be divided, logged and exponentiated, all in O(n log n) with NTT (拓展篇第8章) and Newton's iteration: if B is correct mod xk, one Newton step makes it correct mod x2k. So log n doublings, each a few multiplications of size 2k.

Inverse (P4238): B ← B(2 − AB). Logarithm (needs a0 = 1, P4725): ln A = ∫ A' / A, i.e. derivative, multiply by the inverse, integrate. Exponential (needs a0 = 0, P4726): B ← B(1 − ln B + A). ln and exp turn products into sums: e.g. counting multisets (Euler transform) or "power of a series".

ln and exp of random series with 12 terms, checked against the O(n²) recurrences A·B' = A' (for ln) and E' = A'·E (for exp) computed in Python. Those slow recurrences are also fine in a contest when n is a few thousand.

Newton steps must use A truncated to 2k terms and keep every product truncated to 2k; letting sizes grow makes it O(n log² n) or wrong. ln needs a0 = 1 and exp needs a0 = 0; scale or shift the input first otherwise.

FWT (快速沃尔什变换) computes bitwise convolutions ck = Σi ⊕ j = k aibj for ⊕ ∈ {OR, AND, XOR} in O(n log n) for arrays of length n = 2k: transform both, multiply point by point, transform back, exactly like FFT but with a different butterfly.

OR: forward a[i + half] += a[i] (sum over subsets, SOS DP of 拓展篇第12章), inverse subtracts. AND: a[i] += a[i + half] (sum over supersets). XOR: (x, y) → (x + y, x − y), and the inverse divides by 2 at each level (or by n at the end). P4717.
OR, AND and XOR convolutions of two random arrays of length 8, checked against the O(n²) double loop in Python. With a modulus, the XOR inverse multiplies by the inverse of 2 instead of dividing.

Multipoint evaluation (多点求值) evaluates a degree-n polynomial at n points in O(n log² n): a product tree of (x − xi) and polynomial remainders down the tree. It is rarely needed; know that it exists and that it needs polynomial division (inverse of the reversed divisor).
Polynomial square root (多项式开根): find B with B² ≡ A (mod xⁿ), a0 = 1. Newton iteration doubles the precision each step: B ← (B + A·B⁻¹) / 2 mod x2k, using the inverse from 第 1 节 . O(n log n).

Polynomial power (多项式快速幂) Ak mod xⁿ with a0 = 1: exp(k · ln A) with ln and exp from 第 1 节 , and k may be reduced mod p (it multiplies the series). If a0 ≠ 1, divide out the lowest term c·xt first: Ak = ck xtk (A / (c xt))k, with ck using k mod (p − 1). When a0 is not 1 for a square root, a0 needs a modular square root (Cipolla, NOI 篇第15章).
Checked against the O(n²) coefficient-by-coefficient square root in Python (bk = (ak − Σ bibk−i) / 2). The square root with b0 = 1 is unique, so the two must agree.

title: 单纯形法
summary: Maximise a linear objective under linear constraints by pivoting from vertex to better vertex, detect unboundedness, and know when duality helps.

boxes.text: A linear program (线性规划): maximise c·x subject to Ax ≤ b and x ≥ 0. The optimum, if finite, is attained at a vertex of the feasible polytope. The simplex method (单纯形法) walks from vertex to better neighbouring vertex: pick a variable with positive objective coefficient (entering), find the constraint that limits it first (minimum ratio test: leaving), and pivot. When no coefficient is positive, the current vertex is optimal.

If the entering column has no positive entry, the objective can grow forever: unbounded. If some bi < 0 the origin is not feasible, and an initialisation phase (an auxiliary LP) is needed first. Bland's rule (smallest index) avoids cycling. Exponential in theory, fast in practice.

Each column stands for a variable that is currently non-basic (0); pivoting swaps a basic and a non-basic variable. The first two LPs are checked against trying every vertex (every choice of n tight constraints) with exact fractions in Python; the third, x − y ≤ 2 maximising x + y, is unbounded.

Contest uses: some flow / cut problems are LPs (志愿者招募 P3980 is solved both by min-cost flow and by the simplex method on its dual); duality (max c·x, Ax ≤ b ⇔ min b·y, Aᵀy ≥ c) turns covering problems into packing problems with the same optimum.

Floating-point pivots accumulate error: compare with EPS everywhere and prefer the largest-ratio rule only if cycling is impossible. This version assumes b ≥ 0; with negative b, run the initialisation phase first.

title: 广义后缀自动机
summary: One suffix automaton for many strings: restart from the root for each string and reuse or clone existing transitions instead of creating duplicate states.

boxes.text: A general suffix automaton (广义后缀自动机) accepts every substring of several strings at once. Insert the strings one after another, restarting from the root each time; but when the transition for the next character already exists, do not create a new state: reuse it, or clone it if its length is wrong. Without that check the automaton gets duplicate, unreachable states and counts go wrong (P6139).

Equivalent safe construction: build a trie of all strings, then add trie nodes to the SAM in BFS order, each extending from its parent's state. Distinct substrings of all strings = Σ (len[v] − len[link[v]]), as for one string (拓展篇第3章). Keeping, per state, which strings reach it answers "substrings common to k strings".

Distinct substrings over all strings, checked against putting every substring of every string into a Python set. Strings that are prefixes of each other ("abab" and "ab…") are where the reuse branch matters.

The bug to avoid: plain extend after resetting last = 0 creates a fresh state even when the transition exists, so a string seen before gets a second, disconnected state. That is exactly what the first branch of extend() prevents.

Typical problems: count substrings that occur in at least k of the strings (mark each state with the strings that reach it while walking each string); 诸神眷顾的幻想乡(P3346) builds the general SAM of all root-to- leaf paths of a tree with at most 20 leaves.

title: 计算几何进阶
en: 3D hull, enclosing sphere, Minkowski sums, adaptive Simpson
summary: Grow a 3D hull by deleting the faces a new point sees, find the smallest enclosing sphere, add convex polygons with Minkowski sums, and integrate areas numerically with adaptive Simpson.

boxes.text: The 3D convex hull (三维凸包) is made of triangular faces. Incremental construction: start with a tetrahedron, then add points one by one. A face is visible from the new point p if p lies on its outer side (positive triple product). Delete all visible faces; the edges on the border between visible and invisible faces (the "horizon") each form a new face with p. O(n²) total, enough for n ≤ 2000 (P4724).

Mark visibility per directed edge: for each face (a, b, c) visible from p, set vis[a][b] = vis[b][c] = vis[c][a]. An edge (a, b) of a kept face with vis[b][a] set is a horizon edge, and the new face is (a, b, p) with the same orientation. Perturb the points by about 10⁻⁹ first, so that no four points are coplanar.

A 2 × 2 × 2 cube (surface 24) with random points inside, and a corner tetrahedron (three right triangles of area 4.5 plus an equilateral face of side 3√2): the exact areas are computed by formula in Python. Interior points must not change the area.

The minimum enclosing sphere (最小球覆盖) extends the random incremental circle of 拓展篇第15章 one level deeper: shuffle the points; whenever point i is outside the current sphere, restart with i on the boundary; inside that, whenever j is outside, restart with i and j on the boundary; then k; then l, where four boundary points fix the sphere. Expected O(n) after shuffling.
The sphere through 2 points: centre at the midpoint. Through 3: the circumcircle centre in their plane. Through 4: solve the 3 × 3 linear system |c − pi|² = |c − p0|² (Gaussian elimination, 进阶篇第22章).

The corners of a 4 × 4 × 4 cube plus interior points need the sphere of radius 2√3 (half the space diagonal); two points 10 apart need radius 5. Both answers are exact formulas, independent of the program.

Degenerate input (three collinear points, four coplanar points) makes circum3 / circum4 divide by zero; real solutions either perturb the points or check the determinant and fall back to the smaller case.

The Minkowski sum (闵可夫斯基和) A + B = {a + b} of two convex polygons is convex, and its edges are the edges of A and B sorted by angle. Start both at their lowest (then leftmost) vertex and merge the two edge lists like merge sort, comparing directions by cross product: O(n + m).

Typical uses: "can polygon B moved by vector v touch A?" ⇔ v ∈ A + (−B) (P4557 战争), distances between convex polygons, and motion planning. Remove collinear vertices afterwards if the problem wants a strict polygon.
Two random convex polygons, checked against the convex hull of all n·m pairwise sums in Python (same vertex count and doubled area).

Adaptive Simpson integration (自适应辛普森): Simpson's rule ∫lr f ≈ (r − l)(f(l) + 4f(m) + f(r)) / 6. Compare the whole interval with its two halves; if they agree within 15·ε accept, otherwise recurse on each half with ε / 2. The function only needs to be evaluable, not integrable by hand.

Classic use: the area of a union of circles (or other shapes) as ∫ f(x) dx, where f(x) = total length of the union of the vertical chords at x (merge intervals). Integrate each connected x-range separately (f = 0 in gaps fools the error test), and force a few levels of recursion before trusting the error estimate.
Five random circles, checked against an exact union area in Python (Green's theorem over the arcs not covered by other circles). The minimum depth 8 stops an early, lucky agreement on a coarse split.

Simpson assumes f is smooth; at chord ends f has √ cusps, which is why the adaptive version (not a fixed number of slices) is needed. ε too small makes it slow: pick it a few digits below the required precision.

Voronoi diagram and Delaunay triangulation (Voronoi 图 / Delaunay 三角剖分): the Voronoi cell of a site is the set of points nearest to it; joining sites whose cells share an edge gives the Delaunay triangulation (no point inside any triangle's circumcircle). Both have O(n) size and are built in O(n log n) (divide and conquer or Fortune's sweep). The Euclidean MST is a subgraph of the Delaunay triangulation.

title: 图论补充三
en: Gomory–Hu, block-cut tree, modular shortest paths, k-th shortest path, global min cut, Borůvka
summary: All-pairs min cuts from n − 1 flows, the tree of blocks that tells which vertices every path must use, reachable totals by shortest paths on residues, and easy colouring on chordal graphs.

boxes.text: A Gomory–Hu tree (最小割树) of an undirected weighted graph is a tree on the same vertices such that, for every pair u, v, the minimum u–v cut in the graph equals the smallest edge on the tree path u–v. It needs only n − 1 max-flow runs and then answers all n² min-cut queries.

Gusfield's simple construction: parent[i] = 1 for all i. For i = 2 … n: compute the min cut between i and parent[i] (weight w, side S containing i); set the tree edge (i, parent[i], w); for every j > i with parent[j] = parent[i] and j ∈ S, set parent[j] = i. No graph contraction needed (P4897).

After the last BFS of a max flow, the vertices still reachable from the source (level ≥ 0) are its side of the minimum cut, which is exactly what Gusfield needs. Every query is checked against a separate Edmonds– Karp min cut in Python.

The block-cut tree (圆方树): for every vertex-biconnected block (进阶篇第12章) create a "square" node and connect it to the "round" nodes (original vertices) of the block. The result is a tree. Every simple path u–v in the graph uses exactly the blocks on the tree path between u and v, and the vertices that every u–v path must pass are the round nodes on that tree path.

So "how many vertices lie on all u–v paths" (道路相遇 P4320) = number of round nodes on the tree path = (path length in nodes + 1) / 2. Build it with the same Tarjan stack as vertex_bcc.cpp, creating a square node per popped block.

Checked in Python by the definition: a vertex w lies on every u–v path iff it is u, v, or deleting it disconnects them. On the tree, round and square nodes alternate, so a path with L edges has L/2 + 1 round nodes.

Shortest paths modulo a number (同余最短路): which totals can be written as ax + by + cz with x, y, z ≥ 0? Work modulo a (the smallest step): for each residue r mod a, let d[r] = the smallest reachable total ≡ r. Then every d[r] + k·a is reachable too. The d[r] are shortest paths on a graph of a vertices: r → (r + b) mod a with weight b, r → (r + c) mod a with weight c.
Count reachable totals ≤ h: Σr (⌊(h − d[r]) / a⌋ + 1) over residues with d[r] ≤ h. Graph size a, not h, so h can be 2⁶³ (跳楼机 P3403: floors reachable from floor 1).
Checked against listing every reachable floor in Python. Using the smallest step as the modulus keeps the graph smallest.
The same idea answers "the largest total that cannot be made" (with gcd 1): max over r of d[r] − a.

A graph is chordal (弦图) if every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord. Equivalently it has a perfect elimination ordering: an order where each vertex's later neighbours form a clique. Maximum cardinality search (MCS): repeatedly number the unnumbered vertex with the most numbered neighbours; reversing that order gives a perfect elimination ordering exactly when the graph is chordal.

On chordal graphs many hard problems become easy: the chromatic number equals the maximum clique, which is max over v of (1 + number of earlier-numbered neighbours in MCS order); greedy colouring along the perfect elimination order achieves it (神奇的国度 P3196).
A random chordal graph (each new vertex joined to a clique), checked against trying every colouring in Python. Labels only increase, so stale bucket entries are skipped instead of deleted.

Planar graphs and duality (平面图与对偶图): in a planar graph each face becomes a dual vertex and each edge a dual edge between its two faces. A minimum s–t cut in the planar graph equals a shortest path between the two outer faces in the dual, which turns huge grid min-cuts into Dijkstra (狼抓兔子 P4001).

k-th shortest path (k 短路 , walks may repeat vertices): run Dijkstra from t on the reversed graph to get h(v) = dist(v, t), an exact heuristic. Then run A* from s with key g + h(v): the i-th time t is popped, g is the i-th shortest path length. Each vertex needs to be expanded at most k times.

A* is O(k · m log) in the worst case and is what most solutions use. The guaranteed method builds the shortest-path tree to t; every path is the tree path plus a list of "side-track" edges with cost w + h(v) − h(u), kept in persistent leftist heaps (第5章), giving O((n + m) log m + k log k) (P2483).
The k = 8 shortest walks from 1 to n, checked against a plain best-first enumeration without the heuristic in Python. The heuristic changes only the order of work, not the answers.

Stoer–Wagner (全局最小割): the minimum cut over all ways to split an undirected graph into two nonempty parts, with no fixed source or sink. One phase grows a set A by repeatedly adding the vertex most tightly connected to A; the last two added, s and t, satisfy: the weight of t to the rest is the minimum s–t cut. Record it, merge s and t, repeat n − 1 times.
O(n³) with an adjacency matrix (O(nm + n² log n) with a heap). It beats running max flow n − 1 times, and the code is shorter (P5632).
Checked against trying all 2ⁿ − 2 splits in Python.

Borůvka: in each round, every component picks its cheapest outgoing edge, and all picked edges are added at once. Each round at least halves the number of components, so there are O(log n) rounds. Break ties by edge index so that the picked edges never form a cycle.

Its power is that a round only needs "the cheapest edge leaving each component", which can be found without listing the edges: on a complete graph with weight ai xor aj use a trie (CF888G Xor-MST), on points use geometry. That gives MSTs of graphs with n² implicit edges in O(n log² n).
Checked against Kruskal in Python on the same random graph.
Euler's formula for planar graphs (平面图欧拉公式): a connected planar graph drawn without crossings has V − E + F = 2 (F counts the outer face). With C connected components: V − E + F = 1 + C.

Typical uses: count the regions cut out by segments or chords (build the planar graph: intersections become vertices, then F = E − V + C + 1), prove that a graph is not planar (K5: E = 10 > 9), and bound edge counts so O(E) algorithms on planar graphs are O(V). With the dual graph (第 4 节) it turns planar minimum cuts into shortest paths.

title: 数据结构补充三
en: Cat tree, historic maximum, dynamic centroid, second-offline Mo, zkw, segment tree split
summary: O(1) static range queries with precomputed half-answers, historic maxima with a "best pending prefix" tag, full code for dynamic centroid decomposition, and the idea behind second-offline Mo.

boxes.text: A cat tree (猫树) answers static range queries in O(1) for any associative merge whose partial results can be precomputed. Build a segment tree over a power-of-two length. At each node with midpoint mid, store the answer for every suffix [i, mid] of the left half and every prefix [mid + 1, j] of the right half. A query [l, r] with l ≠ r uses the node where l and r are first split, which is found from the highest differing bit of l and r.

O(n log n) memory and preprocessing, O(1) per query, no LCA walk. For maximum subarray sum each stored entry holds the best inside, the best touching the middle, and the sum. Knapsack-like merges (好吃的题目 P6240) store a whole DP array per position, so queries cost the merge of two arrays.
Maximum subarray sum on random ranges, checked against trying every subarray in Python. The highest bit where l and r differ tells the depth of their split node directly: no tree walk at all.

Historic maximum (区间历史最值): besides the current values ai, ask for max over time of ai. With range add, each node keeps mx (current max) and hmx (historic max), and two lazy tags: add (total pending addition) and hadd (the largest prefix of that pending sequence of additions). When pushing tags (add, hadd) onto a child: child.hmx = max(child.hmx, child.mx + hadd), child.hadd = max(child.hadd, child.add + hadd), then child.mx += add, child.add += add.

The order matters: the historic values must be updated with the child's old current values before adding. That "max prefix of pending additions" tag is the whole trick; CPU 监控(P4314) adds assignment tags the same way, and P6242 combines it with chmin (NOI 篇第5章).
Random range adds (positive and negative), current maxima and historic maxima, checked against tracking every element's best value in Python.

Dynamic centroid decomposition with code (拓展篇第27章 gave the idea): query "sum of values within distance k of x" with point updates (震波 P6329). For each centroid c keep two Fenwick trees indexed by distance: Fc[d] = total value at distance d from c inside c's piece, and Gc[d] = total value inside c's piece at distance d from c's centroid parent.

Query(x, k): start with Fx up to k; then for each centroid ancestor p of the current c: add Fp up to k − dist(x, p), and subtract Gc up to k − dist(x, p) (those vertices were already counted below). Update changes O(log n) Fenwick entries the same way. dist uses the original tree (LCA).

Random queries and point changes, checked against BFS distances from x in Python. Each Fenwick tree is as long as its piece, so the total memory is O(n log n). P6329 additionally XORs each query with the last answer (forced online), which this structure handles directly.

Second-offline Mo (莫队二次离线): when moving a Mo pointer costs O(log n) (e.g. "count pairs i < j in the window with ai > aj", 莫队二次离线 P4887), write each pointer move's contribution as f(prefix, x): "the effect of element x against the prefix 1 … p". Record all those (p, x-range) requests offline, sweep p from 1 to n once with a structure that makes each request O(1), and add the results back. Total O(n√n) instead of O(n√n log n).

Top trees (Top Tree) maintain path and subtree information on a dynamic forest at once, generalising LCT (拓展篇第14章); they are almost never required in contests: LCT plus "virtual subtree" sums (keeping the sum of non-preferred children) covers subtree queries in practice.

zkw segment tree (zkw 线段树 , bottom-up): put the leaves at positions M + i where M is a power of two ≥ n + 2, parents at i / 2. A point update walks up with p >>= 1. A range query [l, r] starts from the open ends l − 1 and r + 1 and moves both up until they become siblings, adding the sibling subtrees they pass.

No recursion, so it is several times faster than the usual segment tree, and about 10 lines. Range updates with lazy tags are possible but awkward; use it for point update + range query (or range update + point query).
Random point additions and range sums, checked against a Python list. The leaf positions M and M + n + 1 are never used by data, which is why M ≥ n + 2.

Segment tree splitting (线段树分裂) is the reverse of merging (拓展篇): to move the values in [x, y] out of a dynamic (value-indexed) segment tree into a new tree, walk down both at once. A node fully inside [x, y] is moved by pointer, not copied; partially covered nodes are split into a new node for each side. Each split creates O(log n) nodes.

With merge and split together, sets of values can be cut and glued freely: "move these values to a new set / merge set t into p / count / k-th" (P5494). Merging costs are paid by the nodes they remove, splits add O(log n), so the total stays O((n + q) log n).
The P5494 operations (0 split off [x, y] as a new set, 1 merge, 2 add copies, 3 count in range, 4 k-th), run at random and checked against Python dictionaries of counts.

The Chtholly tree (珂朵莉树 , ODT, 颜色段均摊) stores the array as a set of maximal segments [l, r] with one value. split(pos) cuts the segment containing pos so that a new one starts at pos. Range assign = split(r + 1), split(l), erase everything between, insert one segment. Other operations just walk the segments in [l, r].

Fast only when random range assignments keep the number of segments small (expected O(n log log n) total, CF896C). Any operation that walks segments costs their count, so without assignments, or on adversarial data, it degrades to O(n) per operation. Always split(r + 1) before split(l): the other order can invalidate the first iterator.
The four CF896C operations (add, assign, x-th smallest, Σ aᵢˣ mod y) at random, checked against a plain Python list.

title: 字符串补充三
en: KMP automaton, Lyndon factorisation, tree hashing
summary: Count strings avoiding a pattern with the KMP automaton and matrix power, split a string into Lyndon words with Duval's algorithm, and test tree isomorphism by hashing from the centroid.

boxes.text: The KMP automaton (KMP 自动机) turns a pattern of length m into states 0 … m ("how many characters of the pattern currently match") with a transition for every character: go[j][c] = j + 1 if p[j+1] = c, else go[nxt[j]][c] (with go[0][c] = 0 on a mismatch). It is the one-pattern case of the AC automaton (拓展篇第2章).

Counting strings of length n that avoid the pattern: DP over (length, state), never entering state m. When n is huge (GT 考试 P3193: n up to 10⁹), the transition is the same every step, so build the (m × m) transition matrix and raise it to the n-th power (进阶篇第22章): O(m³ log n).
Digit strings of length n that do not contain the pattern, modulo K; checked by listing all 10ⁿ strings in Python for small n. The matrix entry T[j][k] counts digits that move state j to state k.

A Lyndon word is strictly smaller than all of its proper suffixes (equivalently, than all its rotations), e.g. "aab", "abb". Every string splits uniquely into Lyndon words w1 ≥ w2 ≥ … ≥ wk (Chen–Fox–Lyndon).

Duval: i = start of the current block, j = compare position, k = scan position. While s[k] ≥ s[j]: if equal, advance both (a repeat of a Lyndon word is forming); if larger, j = i (the whole prefix becomes one longer Lyndon word). When s[k] < s[j], output copies of length k − j and restart after them. The minimal rotation of a string starts at the last Lyndon factor of s + s that begins in the first half (P1368 工艺).
Prints the end position of every factor (P6114 combines these into one XOR). Checked against the definition in Python: repeatedly take the longest prefix that is a Lyndon word.

Tree hashing (树哈希) decides whether two trees are isomorphic. For a rooted tree, compute each vertex's hash from the multiset of its children's hashes, in a way that does not depend on their order, e.g. h(u) = 1 + Σ f(h(child)) with a fixed scrambling function f (xor-shift on 64-bit), or by sorting the children's hashes.

For unrooted trees, root at the centroid (there are one or two): two trees are isomorphic iff their hashes rooted at their centroids match (taking the smaller of two). A plain sum of child hashes collides easily; the scrambling function f is what makes it reliable (树同构 P5043).

Each tree is given by parents of vertices 2 … n. For each tree print the first earlier tree it is isomorphic to. Checked in Python by the canonical bracket encoding (sorted child strings, minimised over all roots), which is exact.

Ukkonen's algorithm builds a suffix tree online in O(n) using an "active point" and suffix links between internal nodes. It is long and fragile; in contests use the suffix automaton of the reversed string (whose link tree is the suffix tree, 拓展篇第33章) or a suffix array instead.

The subsequence automaton (序列自动机): nxt[i][c] = the first position j > i with sj = c (0 if none), filled from the back in O(n · Σ). Testing whether t is a subsequence of s is then one jump per character, O(|t|); it greedily takes the earliest match, which is always safe.

The automaton is a DAG whose paths from state 0 are exactly the distinct subsequences, so DP on it counts them: f(i) = 1 + Σc f(nxt[i][c]), answer f(0) − 1 for nonempty ones. Common subsequences of two strings = paths in both automata at once (P5826 is the template).
Subsequence tests and the count of distinct nonempty subsequences, checked in Python by listing all 2¹² subsequences of s.

2D hashing (二维哈希): hash each row's windows of width b with base P (unsigned overflow as mod 2⁶⁴), then hash each column of those row hashes over windows of height a with a second base Q. A matrix window then has one number, compared to the pattern's in O(1): counting occurrences of an a × b pattern in an n × m text is O(nm).

Same rules as 1D hashing (拓展篇): two different bases for the two directions, and use two moduli or random bases if the problem is adversarial. Prefix-sum style 2D hashes H(i, j) also allow any submatrix in O(1): H = h(x2, y2) − h(x1, y2)·Qa − h(x2, y1)·Pb + h(x1, y1)·PbQa.
Counts occurrences of a 2 × 2 pattern (cut from the text itself, so there is at least one) in a random a/b grid, checked by direct comparison in Python.

title: 反演与容斥
en: Binomial and Stirling inversion, min-max inclusion-exclusion
summary: Turn "at least k" counts into "exactly k" with binomial inversion, switch between block counts with Stirling inversion, and compute an expected maximum from expected minima.

boxes.text: Binomial inversion (二项式反演): if f(k) = Σi≥k C(i, k) g(i) for all k ("f counts objects with at least k marked items, each counted once per chosen k-subset"), then g(k) = Σi≥k (−1)i−k C(i, k) f(i) ("exactly k").

"Exactly k" is hard, "at least k" is easy: choose k items to force the property, arrange the rest freely. Derangements are the case k = 0. 已经没有什么好害怕的了(P4859): count pairings with exactly (n + k)/2 pairs where the candy beats the pill: DP the forced pairs, multiply by (n − j)! for the rest, then invert.
Checked against trying all n! pairings in Python. Sorting both lists lets each a choose among the b's smaller than it, minus those already used by earlier (smaller) a's.

Stirling inversion (斯特林反演) is the analogue with Stirling numbers: f(n) = Σ S(n, k) g(k) ⇔ g(n) = Σ (−1)n−k s(n, k) f(k), where S and s are Stirling numbers of the second and (unsigned) first kind (进阶篇第20章). It converts between "partitions into any number of blocks" and "exactly k blocks".

Min-max inclusion-exclusion (min-max 容斥): for any finite set S of numbers, max(S) = Σ∅≠T⊆S (−1)|T|+1 min(T). It also holds for expectations, E[max] = Σ (−1)|T|+1 E[min(T)], even though max and min of random variables are not linear. The point: E[min] is often easy when E[max] is not.

按位或(P3175): each second a random number i (probability pi) is ORed into x; expected time until all n bits are set. Tb = time bit b first appears; the answer is E[max Tb]. min over a bit set T is the first time any bit of T appears: geometric with success probability 1 − Σi ∩ T = ∅ pi, i.e. 1 − (sum of p over subsets of T's complement), which SOS DP (拓展篇第12章) gives for all T at once.
Checked against solving the Markov chain over all 2ⁿ states with exact fractions in Python. If some bit can never be set, every T containing it has a zero success probability: the answer is INF.

title: 数论补充三
en: Floor sums, primitive roots, square roots mod p, Pick, universal Euclid
summary: Sum floors of linear functions in logarithmic time, find generators modulo a prime, take square roots modulo p with Cipolla, and count lattice points with Pick's theorem.

boxes.text: Floor sums (类欧几里得): f(a, b, c, n) = Σi=0..n ⌊(a·i + b)/c⌋ in O(log) time. If a ≥ c or b ≥ c, pull out the whole parts: ⌊a/c⌋·n(n+1)/2 + ⌊b/c⌋·(n + 1) + f(a mod c, b mod c, c, n). Otherwise, with m = ⌊(a·n + b)/c⌋, count lattice points the other way: f = n·m − f(c, c − b − 1, a, m − 1). The parameters shrink like Euclid's algorithm.
It counts lattice points under a line, so it appears in sums like Σ ⌊(ai + b)/c⌋, Σ i·⌊…⌋ and Σ ⌊…⌋² (the full
Checked against adding every term in Python. When m = 0 the recursive call gets n = −1 and returns 0 through the a ≥ c branch or the formula; the a = 0 case stops the recursion.
Products like a·n and n·m can exceed long long for inputs near 10⁹; use __int128 or a modulus in real problems.

A primitive root (原根) g modulo a prime p generates every non-zero residue: g, g², …, gp−1 are all different. Then every x ≠ 0 is gk for a unique k (its discrete log), which turns multiplication into addition (序列统计 in 拓展篇第8章 , and NTT's g = 3 for 998244353).

Test a candidate g: g is a primitive root iff g(p−1)/q ≠ 1 for every prime factor q of p − 1. Primitive roots are common (φ(p − 1) of them), so trying g = 2, 3, … finds the smallest quickly. Primitive roots exist exactly for 1, 2, 4, pᵏ and 2pᵏ (P6091 lists all of them).
The smallest primitive root of each prime, checked in Python by the same criterion with factors found by trial division (and the known value 3 for 998244353).
Order of g = the smallest d with gd ≡ 1; it always divides p − 1, which is why testing the maximal proper divisors (p − 1)/q is enough.

A quadratic residue (二次剩余) modulo an odd prime p is n with x² ≡ n solvable. Euler's criterion: n(p−1)/2 ≡ 1 if it is a residue, −1 if not. Cipolla's algorithm finds x: pick random a with a² − n a non- residue (half of all a work), set ω² = a² − n, and compute (a + ω)(p+1)/2 in the field of numbers u + vω. The result has v = 0 and is a square root of n (P5491).
The two roots are x and p − x. Arithmetic in u + vω: (u₁ + v₁ω)(u₂ + v₂ω) = (u₁u₂ + v₁v₂ω²) + (u₁v₂ + u₂v₁)ω.
Checked against squaring every residue in Python. P5491 prints the roots in increasing order, or Hola! when none exists.
For p ≡ 3 (mod 4) there is a shortcut: x = n(p+1)/4. Cipolla handles every odd prime.

Pick's theorem (皮克定理): for a polygon whose vertices are lattice points, area = I + B/2 − 1, where I is the number of lattice points strictly inside and B the number on the boundary. A segment from (x₁, y₁) to (x₂, y₂) contains gcd(|x₂ − x₁|, |y₂ − y₁|) + 1 lattice points, so B is a sum of gcds and I follows from the shoelace area.
Electric Fences (P2735): the triangle (0, 0), (n, m), (p, 0); count the lattice points strictly inside: I = A − B/2 + 1 with 2A = p·m.
Checked against testing every lattice point in the bounding box in Python. Each edge contributes gcd points without counting its starting vertex twice.
Working with 2A keeps everything an integer: I = (2A − B + 2) / 2.

Universal Euclid (万能欧几里得): walk along the line y = (p·x + r) / q for x = 1..n and write "U" each time y passes an integer and "R" at each integer x. The string of U's and R's is built by a Euclid-like recursion in O(log) multiplications, if the quantity you want is a monoid: a node that knows how to combine two pieces of the walk.

类欧几里得(第 1 节) needs a new formula for every sum; universal Euclid needs only the merge rule. Below, a node stores (#R, #U, Σy, Σx·y) over its R steps; merging shifts the right part by the left part's counts. Matrices also form a monoid, which gives Σ Ax B⌊(px+r)/q⌋.
Each line prints Σ⌊(px + r)/q⌋ and Σ x·⌊(px + r)/q⌋ for x = 1..n, checked by direct summation in Python. In real problems the fields are taken modulo a prime; here the values fit in long long.

title: BM 算法与多点求值
summary: Recover the shortest linear recurrence of a sequence from its first terms, and evaluate a polynomial at many points with a product tree and polynomial remainders.

boxes.text: Berlekamp–Massey finds the shortest linear recurrence ai = Σj=1..L cj ai−j (mod a prime) that generates a given sequence, in O(n²). Process terms one by one; when the current recurrence predicts ai wrongly by a discrepancy Δ, correct it with a scaled, shifted copy of the recurrence that was current at the last failure.

Contest use: when an answer sequence is known to satisfy some linear recurrence (DP with fixed transitions, matrix powers, counting walks), compute the first few hundred terms by brute force, run BM, then get the n-th term by matrix power or, faster, polynomial "Kitamasa" reduction (P5487).
A sequence made by a third-order recurrence and the Fibonacci numbers: BM recovers orders 3 and 2, and the next five terms match those computed directly in Python.

Feed enough terms: at least 2L for an order-L recurrence, plus a margin, or BM may return a shorter recurrence that fits only the prefix. Work modulo a prime (the algorithm divides by the old discrepancy).

Multipoint evaluation (多项式多点求值): evaluate a degree-n polynomial A at n points in O(n log² n). Build a product tree: leaves (x − xi), each node the product of its children. Then go down: A mod (root product), and at each node reduce the parent's remainder modulo the node's product. At leaf i the remainder is the constant A(xi).

Polynomial division with remainder (O(n log n)): reverse A and B, multiply reversed A by the inverse (NOI 篇第7章) of reversed B modulo xdeg A − deg B + 1 to get the reversed quotient Q; then R = A − Q·B.
A random polynomial evaluated at 9 random points, checked against Horner's rule in Python. Coefficients are listed from x⁰ upward; tree nodes store the products (x − xi) over their ranges.

title: DP 优化补充
en: Slope trick, D&C optimisation, (max,+) matrices, plug DP
summary: Keep a convex DP as its breakpoints in a heap, compute layered DPs with monotone split points by divide and conquer, and power matrices over the (max, +) semiring.

boxes.text: Slope trick keeps a DP whose value is a convex piecewise-linear function f(x) of one variable, not as an array but as the multiset of its breakpoints (points where the slope changes by 1). Adding |x − a| inserts a at both sides; taking a prefix minimum ("x may only increase") throws away the right side. A priority queue stores the breakpoints, so each step is O(log n).

Classic: make an array non-decreasing with the fewest ±1 changes (P4597). fi(x) = min cost with bi = x. Keep a max-heap: push ai; if the top t > ai, pay t − ai, pop t and push ai again. The answer is the total paid.
Checked against the O(n·V) DP over final values in Python. The heap holds where the slope of f changes; its top is the point where f is smallest.
Other slope-trick moves: adding a constant to all breakpoints (shift), keeping two heaps for both sides with lazy offsets, and merging heaps along a tree for tree versions.

Divide-and-conquer optimisation (分治优化): for f[g][i] = minj<i f[g−1][j] + cost(j, i), when the best j (opt) is monotone in i, compute the middle i first by scanning its whole allowed range of j, then recurse on the left half with j ≤ opt(mid) and on the right half with j ≥ opt(mid). Each layer costs O(n log n) instead of O(n²).

Monotone opt holds when cost satisfies the quadrangle inequality (拓展篇第20章); "sum of the segment squared" does. Splitting into k groups with the smallest Σ (group sum)² is 征途(P4072, which also has a slope-optimisation solution).
Twelve random values split into 4 groups; checked against the O(k n²) DP in Python. The recursion depth is log n and each level of one layer scans O(n) candidates in total.

Matrix power in the (max, +) semiring (广义矩阵乘法): replace "multiply" by "+" and "add" by "max": C[i][j] = maxk (A[i][k] + B[k][j]). It is still associative, so fast power works (进阶篇第22章). AL[i][j] is the heaviest walk of exactly L edges from i to j; with (min, +) it is the lightest.

Missing edges are −∞ (for max) or +∞ (for min); identity has 0 on the diagonal and −∞ elsewhere. This semiring view is also the engine behind dynamic DP (第21章): a DP step that is "max over choices of a sum" is a (max, +) matrix product.
Heaviest walk of exactly 7 edges in a random weighted digraph ("x" = no edge), checked by step-by-step DP in Python.

Plug DP (插头 DP, broken-profile DP on connectivity): process the grid cell by cell; the state is the row of m + 1 "plugs" crossing the boundary between processed and unprocessed cells. To count Hamiltonian cycles (P5056), each plug is 0 (none), 1 (left end of a path) or 2 (right end), like brackets; paths never cross, so the bracket matching tells which ends are joined.

At a cell with left plug L and up plug U: (0,0) start a new path going down and right (1, 2); one plug: continue it down or right; (1,1) or (2,2): join two paths, and the partner bracket of one end changes; (2,1): join simply; (1,2): closes a loop, allowed only at the last free cell. States are stored in a hash map, base 4.

Three grids, checked against a Python DFS that counts Hamiltonian cycles directly (each cycle found twice, once per direction). The bracket search starts at the plug itself, so the plug being changed is found as its own partner's match.

Shift the state by one plug at the start of each row (the right plug of the last cell is always 0). Use 64-bit states once m + 1 plugs need more than 32 bits, and a hand-written hash table if unordered_map is too slow.

title: 根号分治、哈希与 bitset
summary: Treat small and large parameters differently around √n, summarise multisets by random weights, and divide boolean work by 64 with bitsets.

boxes.text: Square-root splitting by a threshold (根号分治): when a parameter x makes one approach cheap for small x and another cheap for large x, pick B ≈ √n and use each where it is fast. Example (哈希冲突

The same split by degree: in a graph, "heavy" vertices (degree > √m) are few (at most 2√m), so precompute for them and brute-force light ones; triangle counting in O(m√m) works this way. Both halves cost O(√n) per operation.
Random queries and changes checked against summing directly in Python. Index 0 is skipped in the direct loop because positions start at 1.

Hashing sets with random weights: give every value v a random 64-bit weight r(v). Then the multiset of a segment is summarised by Σ r(ai) (sum hashing) or ⊕ r(ai) (XOR hashing), both available from prefix sums in O(1). XOR cancels pairs, so "every value appears an even number of times" ⇔ prefix XORs are equal at both ends.

Sum hashing checks "is this segment a permutation of 1 … k" (compare with Σ r(1..k)), "do two segments contain the same multiset", and graph conditions like "every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge" (星战
Counts subarrays in which every value occurs an even number of times; checked by testing every subarray in Python.
With plain values instead of random weights, 1 ⊕ 2 ⊕ 3 = 0 would wrongly look "even". Random weights make such accidents practically impossible.

Bitset optimisation: a std::bitset packs 64 booleans per machine word, so shifts, OR, AND and counting run 64 times faster than a bool loop. Subset-sum feasibility: reach |= reach << w for each weight, O(n·S / 64). Transitive closure: if i reaches k then row i |= row k, O(n³ / 64). Gaussian elimination mod 2 XORs whole rows.

The size of a bitset must be a compile-time constant: declare it for the maximum S. Combining bitsets with Mo's algorithm answers "are there two values in the range with difference / sum / product d" (小清新人渣的本愿 P3674).
How many totals from 0 to S can be formed by a subset of the weights; checked with a Python set of reachable sums.
reach.count() counts all set bits at once; (reach >> k)._Find_first() style tricks find the next reachable value. With weights up to 10⁵ and n = 10⁴ this is about 1.5·10⁷ word operations.

Tree blocking (树分块 , 王室联邦 P2325): cut a tree into blocks of size between B and 3B, each with a "capital" such that every block vertex reaches the capital inside the block (the capital itself may lie outside). DFS with a stack: after each child returns, if more than B vertices were pushed since entering u, pop them as one block with capital u. Push u last; leftovers (fewer than B) join the last block.

With B = √n this gives O(√n) blocks of size O(√n) and short paths between capitals: the base of Mo's algorithm on trees with a block order, and of "precompute answers between capitals" methods for path queries.
The answer is not unique, so the output is checked by a validator in Python: every block has between B and 3B vertices, and block ∪ {capital} is connected in the tree.

title: 树状数组技巧、DFS 序与可持久化 Trie
summary: Find the k-th element by walking down a Fenwick tree, turn subtrees into ranges with DFS order, and answer range maximum-XOR queries with a persistent 0-1 trie.

boxes.text: Walking down a Fenwick tree (树状数组倒着走 / 树状数组上二分): to find the smallest position p with prefix sum ≥ k, do not binary search with O(log n) queries each (O(log² n)). Instead build p bit by bit from the top: for step = 2⌊log n⌋ down to 1, if p + step ≤ n and t[p + step] < k, move p += step and k −= t[p].

It works because t[p + step] covers exactly (p, p + step] when p is a multiple of 2·step, which holds at every stage of the walk. With a Fenwick tree of value counts this is "k-th smallest in a multiset" in O(log n), the job usually given to a balanced tree.
Random inserts and k-th queries, checked against a sorted Python list.
Deletions are add(x, −1). Values must be in 1 … V (discretise first). The same walk finds "first position where the prefix sum exceeds S" for any non-negative array.

DFS order (DFS 序): number vertices by entry time tin[u] and record tout[u] = the last entry time inside u's subtree. Then the subtree of u is exactly the range [tin[u], tout[u]], so subtree operations become range operations on an array (Fenwick or segment tree).

Combinations with two Fenwick trees: subtree add + single-vertex query (range add, point query); vertex add + subtree sum (point add, range sum); subtree add + subtree sum (range add, range sum, 拓展篇第26章). Path-to-root sums: add v at tin[u] and −v at tout[u] + 1, then a point query at tin[x] sums the values of x's ancestors (Promotion Counting P3605 uses DFS order with a Fenwick tree over values).
Random subtree and vertex updates and queries, checked against walking each subtree in Python. One range-add / range-sum Fenwick pair handles all four operations.

A persistent 0-1 trie (可持久化 Trie): version i = the trie of a1 … ai, built from version i − 1 by copying one root-to-leaf path (like a persistent segment tree, 进阶篇第8章), with a count in every node. Counts of version r minus version l − 1 describe exactly al … ar.

Maximum of x ⊕ ai over i ∈ [l, r]: walk both versions from the top bit, prefer the opposite bit of x whenever the count difference there is positive. With prefix XORs it answers "maximum XOR of a suffix ending in a range" (最大异或和 P4735).
Values below 2⁶ here (BITS = 6) to keep the test small; use 30 or 31 bits for real inputs. Checked against trying every i in Python.
Node 0 is the empty trie (count 0), so version 0 needs no build and missing children read as 0, as in the persistent segment tree.

A prefix linear basis (前缀线性基) answers "maximum xor of a subset of a[l..r]" online. Keep, for every prefix r, a basis where each vector remembers the largest position it comes from. When inserting ar with position r, at each bit where the stored vector is older, swap them (the newer one stays, the older one continues down).

Then the basis of prefix r restricted to vectors with position ≥ l spans exactly the xors of a[l..r]. Query: greedy from the high bit, using only vectors with pos ≥ l. O(log V) per insert and query (CF1100F Ivan and Burgers).
Checked against building a fresh basis of a[l..r] for every query in Python.

Binary search on a segment tree (线段树上二分): to find the first index i ≥ l with ai ≥ x, do not binary search outside with O(log n) queries each (O(log² n)). Walk the tree once: skip any node outside [l, n] or with max < x; otherwise go left first, then right. O(log n), because only O(log n) nodes are partly inside and each full node is entered only if its answer is there.
The same walk finds the k-th one (descend by counts), the first prefix with sum ≥ s (descend by sums, 第 1 节 is the Fenwick version), and the last index ≤ r satisfying a condition (go right first).
Random updates and "first index ≥ l with value ≥ x" queries, checked against a linear scan in Python.

title: 二分图匹配进阶
en: KM, Hall's theorem, Hopcroft–Karp, stable marriage
summary: Find the maximum-weight perfect matching with labels and slacks, decide matching existence with Hall's condition, match large graphs in O(m√n) with Hopcroft–Karp, and find stable marriages.

boxes.text: Maximum-weight perfect matching in a bipartite graph with n + n vertices: the KM algorithm (Kuhn– Munkres, 匈牙利算法的带权版本) keeps labels lx[i] (left) and ly[j] (right) with lx[i] + ly[j] ≥ w(i, j) for every edge. Edges with equality are "tight"; a perfect matching using only tight edges is optimal. When the search for an augmenting path gets stuck, lower lx on the visited left vertices and raise ly on the visited right ones by the smallest slack, which creates a new tight edge.

The BFS version with slack[j] = min over visited i of lx[i] + ly[j] − w(i, j) runs in O(n³) (P6577). Min-cost flow (拓展篇第1章) solves the same problem more slowly but more flexibly; KM is the tool when n ≤ 500 and the graph is complete or dense.
Random weight matrices (including negatives), checked against trying all n! perfect matchings in Python. Starting with lx[i] = the largest weight in row i and ly = 0 satisfies the label condition.
The DFS version of KM is O(n⁴) on bad inputs; use the BFS-with-slack version above. For a maximum- weight matching that need not be perfect, add zero-weight dummy edges first.

Hall's theorem (Hall 定理): a bipartite graph has a matching covering every left vertex iff every set S of left vertices has |N(S)| ≥ |S| (at least as many neighbours). It turns matching questions into inequalities that can be checked with data structures.

Ice Skates (P3488): people of shoe size i may take skates of sizes i … i + d. Hall's condition only needs to be checked on contiguous size ranges: Σl..r (people − k) ≤ k·d for all l ≤ r, i.e. the maximum subarray sum of (counti − k) ≤ k·d, a segment tree with maximum subarray nodes (进阶篇第6章) under point updates.

Hopcroft–Karp: instead of one augmenting path at a time (Hungarian / Kuhn, O(nm)), each phase BFS- layers the graph from all free left vertices, then finds a maximal set of vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths by DFS along the layers. There are only O(√n) phases, so the total is O(m√n).
It is Dinic on the unit-capacity matching network written directly. Use it when n is large (10⁵) and Kuhn is too slow (P3386 in its big-data variants).
Checked against Kuhn's algorithm in Python on a random bipartite graph.

Stable marriage (稳定婚姻 , Gale–Shapley): n men and n women each rank the other side. A matching is stable if no man and woman both prefer each other to their partners. Free men propose down their lists; a woman keeps the best proposer so far and rejects the rest. It ends after at most n² proposals with a stable matching.

The result is proposer-optimal: every man gets the best partner he has in any stable matching (and every woman the worst). P1407 asks the related question whether a given marriage is "unsafe" (an alternating cycle exists), solved with SCC.
Checked in Python by listing all n! matchings, keeping the stable ones, and giving each man his best stable partner: Gale–Shapley must produce exactly that.

title: 动态 DP
summary: Re-answer a tree DP after point changes by writing each heavy-edge step as a (max, +) matrix product kept in a segment tree over heavy-light order.

boxes.text: Dynamic DP (动态 DP): a tree DP must be answered again after each point change. Maximum-weight independent set: f[u][0] = Σ max(f[v][0], f[v][1]), f[u][1] = w[u] + Σ f[v][0]. Split the children into the heavy child s and light children, and collect the light part in g[u][0] = Σlight max(f[v][0], f[v][1]), g[u][1] = w[u] + Σlight f[v][0]. Then the step along the heavy edge is a (max, +) matrix product: (f[u][0], f[u][1]) = [[g0, g0], [g1, −∞]] ⊗ (f[s][0], f[s][1]).

Keep these 2 × 2 matrices in a segment tree over HLD order (拓展篇 / 进阶篇第9章). A chain's product gives the f values of its top. A change at x updates x's matrix, then climbs: each chain top's new f changes its parent's g (a light edge), so O(log n) chains × O(log n) segment tree = O(log² n) per change (P4719).

Random weights (some negative) and point changes; after each change the answer is checked against recomputing the whole tree DP in Python. The chain's last vertex is applied to the vector (0, −∞), so the top's f values are just the first column of the product.

Update g of the parent with the difference between the chain top's new and old f, computed before and after the segment tree update; recomputing g from scratch would cost O(degree). The product order must follow the chain from top to bottom.

A global balanced binary tree (全局平衡二叉树) replaces the segment trees of heavy-light decomposition. For each heavy chain build a binary search tree over the chain, choosing as root the vertex that splits the chain by weight, where a vertex's weight is 1 + the sizes of its light subtrees. Light edges hang the chain trees together into one tree of depth O(log n) in total, not O(log² n).

In dynamic DP (第 1 节) every update walks from a vertex to the root and fixes one matrix per node: with HLD that is O(log² n) segment-tree work, with the global balanced tree it is O(log n). Each node stores the product of the matrices in its BST subtree (its own light-child matrix in the middle); a light-edge step updates the parent chain's light matrix, exactly as in the HLD version. Used for the " 加强版 " (strengthened) dynamic DP problem P4751, where O(log² n) is too slow.
Build by weight, not by count: choosing the middle vertex by count gives O(log² n) depth again. The tree is static: it does not support link / cut (use LCT for that).

title: LGV 引理、整数划分与子集卷积
summary: Count non-intersecting lattice paths with a determinant, compute partition numbers with the pentagonal number theorem, and convolve over disjoint subsets with ranked zeta transforms.

boxes.text: The LGV lemma (Lindström–Gessel–Viennot): in a DAG, take starts A1 … Ak and ends B1 … Bk, and let e(Ai, Bj) = number of paths from Ai to Bj. Then det[e(Ai, Bj)] = Σ over vertex-disjoint path systems of sign(σ), where σ says which start goes to which end.

On a grid moving only right / down with starts and ends in "compatible order" (sorted the same way along a diagonal), every disjoint system uses the identity σ, so the determinant counts the non- intersecting path systems exactly (P6657). Grid path counts are binomials: C(dx + dy, dx).
Two and three paths from the top row to the bottom row of a 4 × 4 grid, checked by listing every combination of paths in Python and keeping the vertex-disjoint ones.

Order matters: if the i-th start is not "left of" the (i+1)-th in the same sense as the ends, crossing systems get sign −1 and the determinant is no longer a count (it can even be negative). Sort starts and ends consistently along the boundary first.

The partition number p(n) (整数划分) counts ways to write n as an unordered sum of positive integers. The simple DP "coins 1 … n" (进阶篇第13章) is O(n²). Euler's pentagonal number theorem: Π (1 − xk) = Σj (−1)j xj(3j−1)/2, so p(n) = Σj≥1 (−1)j+1 (p(n − j(3j−1)/2) + p(n − j(3j+1)/2)): only O(√n) terms each, O(n√n) total.

The generalised pentagonal numbers 1, 2, 5, 7, 12, 15, … come in pairs with signs + +, − −, + +, …. Partitions into distinct parts, or parts with bounds, use similar generating-function tricks (跑步 P6189 has n = 10⁵).
p(10) = 42, p(100) = 190569292, p(2000) mod 10⁹+7, all checked against the O(n²) coin DP in Python.
Keep s as a long long sum of at most 2√n terms below MOD before reducing; the alternating signs need the final (s % MOD + MOD) % MOD.

Subset convolution (子集卷积): c[S] = ΣT⊆S a[T]·b[S∖T], i.e. split S into two disjoint parts. Plain enumeration is 3ⁿ. OR-convolution (NOI 篇第7章) would also allow overlapping parts. Fix it by rank: split a, b by popcount, ai[S] = a[S] if |S| = i; OR-transform each; for each S multiply as polynomials in the rank, ck = Σi+j=k âi·bj; inverse-transform and keep c|S|[S]. O(2ⁿ n²) (P6097).
Why it works: T ∪ U = S with |T| + |U| = |S| forces T and U to be disjoint. Used for DP over subsets where a set splits into disjoint pieces (counting connected subgraphs, set partitions).
Random arrays on 4 bits, checked against enumerating every submask T of every S in Python (the 3ⁿ method). Real problems work modulo a prime, which keeps the intermediate values small.

title: 建图技巧与 Johnson
summary: Replace range edges by O(log n) edges into segment-tree nodes, shrink "at most one" 2-SAT groups with prefix variables, and get all-pairs shortest paths with negative edges by reweighting.

boxes.text: Segment-tree graph building (线段树优化建图): edges "from u to every vertex in [l, r]" (or the reverse) would cost O(n) edges each. Build two segment trees whose nodes are extra vertices: an out-tree with edges parent → child (weight 0), whose leaves are the real vertices, and an in-tree with edges child → parent (weight 0). Then u → [l, r] is u → the O(log n) covering nodes of the out-tree; [l, r] → u goes from the covering nodes of the in-tree to u.

O((n + m log n)) edges in total, then any graph algorithm runs as usual (Dijkstra here, CF786B Legacy; also SCC and 2-SAT). The leaves of both trees must be the same real vertices (or joined by 0-edges), so paths can enter one tree and leave the other.

Type 1: u → v; type 2: u → every vertex in [l, r]; type 3: every vertex in [l, r] → u. Checked against expanding every range into single edges and running Dijkstra in Python. Using the real vertex as the leaf of both trees joins them without extra edges.

2-SAT with "at most one" groups: forbidding every pair inside a group of size k costs O(k²) clauses. Add prefix variables Pi = "some of the first i members is true". Clauses: xi → Pi, Pi−1 → Pi, and Pi−1 → ¬xi (if an earlier member is true, xi must be false). O(k) clauses, the same answers (Riddle P6378).
The same prefix trick (or a segment tree over the literals, 23.1) shrinks any "range of implications" in 2- SAT. Solve with SCCs as in 进阶篇第12章 : unsatisfiable iff some x and ¬x share an SCC.

Random clauses (a negative number means "not") and three groups with at most one true member each; checked against trying all 2⁸ assignments in Python. The node for "v == true" is 2v and for "v == false" is 2v + 1, so its negation is a single XOR with 1.

Johnson's algorithm (Johnson 全源最短路) finds all-pairs shortest paths with negative edges (but no negative cycle) in O(nm log m), better than Floyd's O(n³) on sparse graphs. Add a virtual vertex 0 with 0- edges to all vertices; Bellman-Ford / SPFA gives potentials h(v) = dist(0, v). Reweight w'(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(u) − h(v) ≥ 0, run Dijkstra from every vertex, and undo: dist(u, v) = dist'(u, v) − h(u) + h(v).

Why reweighting keeps shortest paths: along any path u → v the potentials telescope, so every path's length changes by the same h(u) − h(v). And w' ≥ 0 because h(v) ≤ h(u) + w(u, v) (the triangle inequality of shortest distances). A negative cycle shows up in the Bellman-Ford step (P5905).

A random graph with some negative edges, checked against Floyd–Warshall in Python ("x" = unreachable, −1 = a negative cycle exists). Starting every h at 0 is the same as the virtual source with 0-edges.
